# 12. Narrative and worldbuilding

A roguelike kills its protagonist, rebuilds its world and starts again, often dozens or hundreds of times. Story has to work inside that loop. This chapter covers where roguelike stories come from and how players assemble them; how to leave room for imagination; story shapes that survive permadeath; what death and restarting mean in the fiction; how mechanics, numbers, tone, setting and words build a world; how to structure authored story for replay; how to make generated characters, histories and plots read as stories; and how to borrow real symbols and cultures responsibly.

The talks approach narrative from unusually varied directions: working roguelike developers, interactive-fiction authors, academic researchers in story generation, a former playwright, tabletop designers, reality-television analysts and the fans who chronicled Blaseball. Their through-line is that the story a roguelike player remembers is mostly one they put together themselves, so the designer's job is less to tell a story than to build a world that generates, implies and acknowledges stories, and to make sure the fiction and the mechanics say the same thing. Authored narrative still has a place, but only when it is shaped for repetition and death, and when the systems, symbols and tone underneath it are chosen on purpose.

## In brief

- Players remember and retell what the systems did to them, not the scripted beats, and Emilia Lazer-Walker argues that roguelikes are better than any other genre at producing those emergent stories ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 3:58](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=238); [Tarn Adams 2018, 7:18](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=438); [Max Kreminski 2019, 4:57](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=297); [Jim Shepard 2016, 3:16](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=196); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 13:45](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=825)).
- Emergent stories need systems that interlock, behave consistently and can be investigated, plus enough sparseness that players have room to invent the rest ([Tarn Adams 2018, 3:08](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=188); [Chris McCormick 2021, 3:19](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=199); [Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 10:49](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=649)).
- Show less than you know: thin, fragmentary and unexplained material is completed by players' pattern-seeking imagination, and explaining it can take that away ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 13:10](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=790); [Kate Compton 2016, 9:20](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=560); [Cezar Capacle 2024, 9:29](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=569); [Dustin Freeman 2022, 10:53](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=653); [Paul Dean 2025, 17:23](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1043)).
- Treat the game as the player's storytelling partner: start them with a generated situation, keep introducing disruptions, limit undo and options, and remember and call back their small choices ([Max Kreminski 2019, 5:24](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=324); [Max Kreminski 2019, 7:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=461); [Max Kreminski 2019, 8:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=486); [Max Kreminski 2019, 9:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=546); [Max Kreminski 2019, 9:51](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=591); [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 8:02](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=482)).
- Make the player live the story through decisions and play rather than read about it, and where a rule feels arbitrary, a thin layer of matching fiction can make players accept it ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:23](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=203); [Jongwoo Kim 2018, 3:57](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=237); [Jim Shepard 2018, 9:26](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=566); [Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 26:53](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1613); [Jon Perry 2025, 28:21](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1701)).
- Your numbers, categories and generators are worldbuilding, because players read them as facts about the world whether or not you meant them to ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 18:44](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1124); [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=331); [Robin Mendoza 2024, 1:50](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=110); [James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 22:37](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1357)).
- Authored story has to be built for repetition: keep anything that replays every run short, and prefer linear strands or storylets released by conditions across runs over branching trees ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:46](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=826); [Nic Junius 2024, 8:01](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=481); [Nic Junius 2024, 11:15](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=675); [Nic Junius 2024, 18:21](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1101); [Bruno Dias 2016, 15:17](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=917); [Stav Hinenzon 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=226)).
- Generated characters feel authored when generation leads into handwritten material and the game visibly acknowledges what has happened to them, including what happened by chance ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 3:11](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=191); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 18:50](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1130); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 17:00](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1020); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 21:36](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1296)).
- A simulation's output is not yet a story: log what happens, sift it for dramatic patterns, and surface the best moments to the player ([Max Kreminski 2019, 13:29](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=809); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:37](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=337); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:01](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=181); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:28](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=208); [Max Kreminski 2020, 1:34](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=94); [Bad News team 2016, 7:22](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=442)).
- Death and restarting are narrative material: decide whether the restart needs an in-world reason, carry story rather than power across deaths, and let failed runs leave traces in the world ([Harry Solomons 2024, 24:30](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1470); [James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 35:14](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2114); [Tim Keenan 2017, 4:33](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=273); [Jim Shepard 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=818); [Harry Solomons 2024, 10:19](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=619)).

## Where roguelike stories come from

Every game carries two stories. Emilia Lazer-Walker, borrowing Marc Laidlaw's framing, calls them the *embedded* story, the authored content a designer studs into the game, and the *emergent* story, the one that comes out of the player's own choices. Roguelikes can have both, but she argues they are better than any other genre at the second kind, at making space for players to come up with stories of their own ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 3:58](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=238)). The value of player-made stories recurs across the talks from speakers working on very different games, and it is the foundation for everything else in this chapter: in a roguelike, the story the player remembers is mostly one they put together themselves.

### The convergence: players tell stories about what the systems did

Several speakers arrived at the same observation independently. Max Kreminski points to retellings like Boatmurdered (Dwarf Fortress), Alice and Kev (The Sims) and Pro Vercelli (Football Manager) as evidence that some players seek out simulation games primarily as storytelling partners, and relays an academic view that a game succeeds if it drives players to create stories about their experiences ([Max Kreminski 2019, 4:57](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=297)). What he loves about roguelikes, he says, is that a player fumbling around in Dwarf Fortress and dying produces a compelling story even though neither the player nor the game was trying to make one ([Max Kreminski 2020, 0:21](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=21)). Brian Walker describes the story of a Brogue run as the player's path through dense, intense, interlocking zones, chosen by an improvised build: high-intensity zone effects make it exciting, qualitatively varied zones make it novel, and dense interlocking makes the choice of path interesting, so the story is co-authored by the player's choices and the dungeon ([Brian Walker 2016, 24:33](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1473)). Jim Shepard reports that Dungeonmans has almost no authored plot, only a minimal legend of past heroes and a villain, yet when he asks players what the story is they describe what they did. A well-established tone gave them a trellis for their own narratives to grow on ([Jim Shepard 2016, 3:16](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=196)).

The scripted parts, by contrast, are what players do not retell. Tarn Adams notes that people's Skyrim stories are about putting buckets on people's heads, never about the dragon; he has never heard anyone recount a boss battle. Fixed plot events are the same for everybody, so the retellable thread is what the player actually did, and in strategy games it is how the opposition behaved on a randomised map ([Tarn Adams 2018, 7:18](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=438)). Jamie Brittain's best Shiren the Wanderer run ended at the final dragon because his hand was stuck in a pot and he could not fight: an ending no blockbuster would script, produced by chaos flowing through systems ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 13:45](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=825)). Nick Cummings makes the same argument about baseball, which looked rigid on the surface but turned out to be a story-generation engine that only works because of its quirks, frictions and imperfections, conjuring nicknames, odd outcomes and stories at every level of play; he calls the joy in edge cases where rules bump into each other the essential roguelike experience ([Nick Cummings 2026, 53:14](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3194)).

Aaron A. Reed gives this a history. The Hobbit text adventure had simulationist ideas that produced un-Tolkien emergent stories, and the genre that followed treated those as bugs; the ideas were not adopted by text adventures, but they had been living in roguelikes all along ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 22:35](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=1355)). The reason, he says, is that a designer with a specific story to tell finds emergent behaviour breaks it: if the story is about the nobility of elves, picking one up and carrying him around ruins it. He calls The Hobbit a bifurcation point where text adventures could have become more like roguelikes ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 25:21](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=1521)). The choice between control and simulation is old, and roguelikes sit on the simulation side of it.

Xalavier Nelson Jr. puts the consequence for procedural generation bluntly: its value is creating an endless supply of context into which players inject their own meaning ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 10:01](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=601)). Shepard draws the matching conclusion for authored content: however elaborate it is, storytelling is only at its best when the player contributes to the output, so developers should provide seeds and listen ([Jim Shepard 2017, 22:02](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1322)).

> It is about creating context, endless amount of context for people to find their own meaning in. — [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 10:01](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=601)

### Retelling is the evidence

If emergent stories are the goal, how do you know you have them? Florence Smith Nicholls proposes *retellings* as the test: if players are motivated to retell their play experience, the generated experience was interesting or memorable. Some systems even host retellings directly, as Love Island does with its spin-off show and weekly panels, and as Blaseball did with official round-ups that organised its history into eras ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 5:14](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=314)). Shawn Main reports that Riot took exactly this as an early signal that its Lab of Legends roguelike mode was working: players came back saying, in effect, "I had this power and this card, let me tell you about this", and Main attributes those personal stories to combinatorial choices producing sharp power growth in a short time ([Shawn Main 2021, 6:20](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=380)). Watch for players telling you stories: both talks treat it as a signal that the narrative is working.

### The raw ingredients

The talks name a handful of sources from which these stories are made.

**Chaos.** Joel Clark argues narrative is how people rise above and explain things that otherwise make no sense, so allowing more chaos into a design can make the stories told or generated from it better ([Joel Clark 2020, 17:19](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1039)).

**Dice that redirect.** Shawn Main, answering a dungeon master, says what makes critical failures and successes matter is that a single roll can take the story in its own direction; slight over- and under-performance across two hours of rolls does not engage him. The result of one roll becomes the setup for the next story beat ([Shawn Main 2017, 23:12](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1392)).

**Correlations that beg explanation.** Alex Byaly's causal-graph generator produces patterns such as accountants evading more tax or goats never eating mice. Either relationship could have gone the other way and either could be explained, and if he does not supply the explanation, players will: he calls these correlations storytelling fuel ([Alex Byaly 2022, 21:56](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1316)).

**Player mistakes.** Brittain recounts entering a Heat Signature capture mission with only lethal gear and improvising by putting a subverter on a teleport pad to send the target into space for pickup; designer Tom Francis replied that this was the kind of high jinks he hoped for. Brittain describes Heat Signature as a game that relies on the fallibility of how players engage its systems, and sets it against story structures that encourage compliance ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 15:42](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=942)).

**Other players.** Tyriq Plummer argues multiplayer roguelikes produce richer stories than solo deaths: a companion stealing a vital potion and leaving you, hunting them down for revenge, or both ending up cornered. A real human supplies betrayal more cheaply than a simulated relationship would ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=324)).

**Loss and attachment.** Stella Vermilion describes how Nuzlocke losses build emotional attachment to nicknamed party members: in her Brilliant Diamond run one was lost to a critical hit at the grass gym and another deliberately sacrificed so the run could continue, and victory can come only after many sacrifices or across several runs ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:56:18](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32178)).

**Happy accidents.** Generators with many outputs produce coincidences that players read as intended. Elliot Trinidad seeded themed name parts into Blaseball's name generator, hoping, for instance, that "beef" would land on the Dallas Steaks. Then Beef Knight died and was replaced by Flan Prince, a similarly themed name, by one-in-a-million chance, instantly creating backstory and fan speculation. When a generator outputs a hundred things, players connect the dots ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 23:59](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1439)). Plain names have their own value: Blaseball's narrative team wanted more "nobody" characters who could rise purely through generated events, and Mike Townsend went from hated, meme-worthy pitcher to central hero while some main-character names got benched and did nothing ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 14:44](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=884)).

Younès Rabii's Pokemon Glitch, a randomised, glitched Pokémon Gold, is the extreme case. In Sprout Tower, which an NPC says was once a hundred-foot Bellsprout, a monk who should have a level-3 Bellsprout had one at level 131, an illegal level, and fighting it felt like fighting the tower itself ([Younès Rabii 2021, 6:29](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=389)). Cyndaquil evolved through five stages into a plant type, and Rabii made up head canon to explain it: a sequoia that grows from the ashes of forest fires ([Younès Rabii 2021, 8:56](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=536)). The silent final boss Red became "Rocket Red", asked in glitch text for a Pokémon and an attack, took Rabii's ghost Pokémon and its Curse, said the curse was erased and disappeared, closing a story about a hostile, cursed world ([Younès Rabii 2021, 12:25](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=745)). Rabii's conclusion is that these mechanics and this story had no author, not Nintendo, not him, not his program; randomness mixing existing material supplied the right ingredients for a story to form in the player's mind ([Younès Rabii 2021, 13:13](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=793)).

The same mechanism works at the tabletop. Atty Vohra invents a backstory to justify a generated monster's stats, such as a ghost princess tormented by a patriarchal sultanate, and that backstory can seed a quest line to avenge her, weaving random encounters into the campaign's larger narrative ([Atty Vohra 2021, 7:17](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=437)).

### What you have to provide

Emergence is not free. Tarn Adams summarises what produces it: interlocking mechanics that resonate with the outside world, are internally consistent, and let the player investigate. Those produce stories players retell to each other, and he says designers already understand this intuitively from playing such games ([Tarn Adams 2018, 3:08](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=188)). The other half is room. Chris McCormick calls the original Rogue "minimalist perfection": enough going on that it is not boring, but sparse enough to leave the player space to invent their own narrative ([Chris McCormick 2021, 3:19](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=199)).

**In practice:**

- Build systems that interact with each other, behave consistently, and can be probed; these are where retellable events come from ([Tarn Adams 2018, 3:08](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=188); [Brian Walker 2016, 24:33](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1473)).
- Allow outcomes that swing hard, from crits, mistakes and other players, rather than smoothing every result toward the mean ([Shawn Main 2017, 23:12](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1392); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 15:42](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=942)).
- Let generators produce patterns and coincidences without explaining all of them ([Alex Byaly 2022, 21:56](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1316); [Elliot Trinidad 2023, 23:59](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1439)).
- Treat players retelling their runs as the measure of success, and consider giving them a place to do it ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 5:14](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=314)).

## Let the player's imagination do the work

The first roguelike learned this lesson by accident. Glenn Wichman, Michael Toy and Ken Arnold planned for Rogue's monsters to have their own ways of living, perhaps building their own dungeons. Once rooms, letters and stats were in place, the game was effectively done: players were already imagining all of that, and the designers just had to get out of their way ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 10:49](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=649)).

### Thin stimuli, rich stories

A cluster of speakers explain why this works: the player's mind fills gaps and finds patterns. The pattern-finding side is *apophenia*, the human tendency to perceive meaningful patterns in unrelated data, which Cezar Capacle describes directly below. Joseph Hewitt says the mind keeps a mental simulation that fills gaps, so sparse information, as in Bloodborne, can produce elaborate imagined worlds; the player's imagination does much of the world-building ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 13:10](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=790)). Kate Compton's Hip Chef patron generator produces customers like "a nervous nun with haunted eyes" who orders chardonnay and leaves; she says this sketching of text that makes your mind tell stories is, for her, one of the core ingredients of roguelikeness ([Kate Compton 2016, 9:20](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=560)). Cezar Capacle explains why random encounters and oracle results in solo tabletop play do not dissolve into incoherent chaos: pattern-seeking and confirmation bias, harmful in real life, help when creating a story as you go, and players weave the results into a cohesive narrative that sometimes surprises them ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 9:29](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=569)). Dustin Freeman, citing Grotowski-era "poor theatre", reads out a Spirit of the Ages message log in which a bear eats a frog, gains HP, stops being angry and feels social toward you because of a strange mood. Adding explicit story or explanation, he argues, would take away the player's own interpretation, which is where the interesting things happen ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 10:53](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=653)).

> It is the player's imagination that is doing a lot of the heavy lifting to build this game world. — [Joseph Hewitt 2024, 13:10](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=790)

Presentation carries the weight. Shepard argues that a great story shown badly falls apart while a merely okay story presented in a fun way grows on players; information should be shown so players can and choose to retain it, and since roguelike players already do mental lifting with ASCII symbols, you can spell out a lot but not everything ([Jim Shepard 2018, 2:41](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=161)). Santiago Zapata, offering his own reading rather than the developer's, says ADOM handled the fact that computers are not good at storytelling by building a detailed original setting with foundations for several paths, which players might or might not follow, letting their imagination complete a more complex world than earlier games had ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 25:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=1517)). For modular procedural text, Bruno Dias says the writing style itself must change: brief, evocative, not overly detailed, giving small morsels that lead players on so they build their own arcs. That is what lets him generate Voyageur's planets one at a time without fitting them into an overarching narrative ([Bruno Dias 2016, 17:22](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=1042)).

### Give story in fragments and gaps

The practical consequence is that you do not need to tell the whole story, or tell it in order. Paul Dean, writing for Pacific Drive, describes lore that players get the gist of from partial fragments, like archaeology or a jigsaw, citing Horizon Zero Dawn's side quests and lore found in any order; he kept his own lore short, relevant, varied and worth finding ([Paul Dean 2025, 17:23](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1043)). He grounds this in the genre's structure: roguelikes are built on repetition, mirroring and parallels punctuated by novel discoveries that join a bigger picture, so players will meet story elements in any order and linear narrative need not be treated as necessary ([Paul Dean 2025, 14:40](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=880)). A loose narrative with holes, like Stardew Valley's short conversations and parallel threads, invites players to build interpretations from what characters do not say; that fanbase has extrapolated from such gaps for a decade ([Paul Dean 2025, 7:16](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=436)). And you can introduce an idea without explaining it and pay it off later, which creates suspense: stories are not programs that must load every reference up front ([Paul Dean 2025, 3:26](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=206)).

Several devices exploit gaps directly:

- **Cropped descriptions.** Mike Cook compares a good street photograph to FromSoftware-style item descriptions: a partial description of an item, place or person with trails coming off it that suggest a whole society, just as things exist beyond the edge of a photo ([Mike Cook 2026, 6:30](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=390)).
- **Coined vocabulary.** Younès Rabii notes that the novel La Horde du Contrevent constantly coins words without explaining them, evoking a rich world through vibes and interpretation, as Caves of Qud's names suggest a whole creature in a single word ([Younès Rabii 2022, 11:36](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=696)).
- **False rumours.** Leonard Richardson points out that NetHack's fortune-cookie rumours include false ones like "Ever tried enchanting a rope?" when the game has no ropes. One line of text suggests a mechanic that would be expensive to build, expanding the imagined game at almost no cost; he now loves the false rumours more than the true ones ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 7:54](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=474)).

### Order changes meaning

Tim Keenan tested this in Duskers. For the gray goo storyline, one log has a scientist worried about a half-gelatinous dead rat near a replicator, another has operators mocking scientists who panic over replicators. In a web survey that showed the logs in random order, reading the worried scientist first made the rat seem more concerning, though Keenan admits results got noisier with more respondents ([Tim Keenan 2017, 8:48](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=528)). He had planned to dole out a linear backbone story in order, but shuffled the pages and gave them to different people, who formed completely different interpretations. He embraced it: competing theories debated on forums became part of the fun ([Tim Keenan 2017, 14:46](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=886)). If your fragments will arrive in random order anyway, write them so that every order produces a reading, and treat divergent readings as a feature.

Chelsea Thompto sees a related quality in procedural art: it asks audiences to spend longer with a work, which then blossoms in the mind over repeated experience rather than being immediately clear, something she connects to what she loves about roguelikes ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 10:28](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=628)).

### Immersion, frame and cooperation

How fully does the player believe? The talks offer three related positions. Jason Grinblat, drawing on Kristine Jørgensen's *Gameworld Interfaces*, argues players never fully lose themselves: they always know they are a person at a computer who has chosen to inhabit a fictional world, adopting an "illusory attitude" that accepts arbitrary rules as if real. Threshold messages like Diablo II's "I am overburdened" are naturalised conventions for talking across the two worlds, not fourth-wall breaks as they would be in a novel ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 8:16](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=496)). He uses Erving Goffman's frame analysis to read bugs the same way: *keying* transposes meaning between frames, so reading something serious as a joke is up-keying and failing to read a joke as a joke is down-keying, and something that is a leak in one frame may be aesthetically meaningful in another ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 11:52](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=712)). Matt Carney, citing the same book, prefers to think of a game as a resonant object, a tuned bell to which the player brings their own subjectivity, rather than pursuing immersion, which he finds stifling ([Matt Carney 2026, 24:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1498)). Hewitt's view sits alongside both: players know the game is a lie but cooperate with the illusion because they want to be entertained ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 13:10](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=790)).

These views agree more than they differ. None asks you to seal the player inside the fiction; all treat the player as an active, knowing participant who completes the world. The practical difference is emphasis: Grinblat's frame gives you licence to use conventions that cross between game and fiction, Carney's asks you to tune the object and trust the player to resonate with it, and Hewitt's asks you to plant points that stimulate imagination ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 8:16](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=496); [Matt Carney 2026, 24:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1498); [Joseph Hewitt 2024, 13:10](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=790)).

### Write for a world you do not control

Emilia Lazer-Walker gives the craft rule for authored content in an unpredictable world. Janet Cardiff's audio walk mentions a zoo polar bear that may no longer be there: if the bear is present, it seems Cardiff knows where you are; if it is absent, that fits the piece's theme of the passage of time. The text is fixed but equally meaningful whether or not the world matches it ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 12:08](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=728)).

**In practice:**

- Show less than you know. Present events without explanation and let players supply motives ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 10:53](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=653); [Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 10:49](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=649)).
- Write brief, evocative fragments that can be met in any order and leave hooks unexplained ([Bruno Dias 2016, 17:22](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=1042); [Paul Dean 2025, 17:23](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1043); [Paul Dean 2025, 3:26](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=206)).
- Use cheap suggestion devices: cropped descriptions, coined words, rumours of things that may not exist ([Mike Cook 2026, 6:30](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=390); [Younès Rabii 2022, 11:36](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=696); [Leonard Richardson 2017, 7:54](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=474)).
- Write authored lines so they stay meaningful whatever the generated world turns out to be ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 12:08](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=728)).

## Players as co-authors

If players make the stories, the designer's job shifts from writing a story to helping players write theirs. Max Kreminski gives this its clearest frame: games act as storytelling partners by giving players *creativity support*, helping them past four common barriers: fear of the blank canvas, fear of judgment, writer's block and perfectionism ([Max Kreminski 2019, 5:24](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=324)). Each barrier has a design answer.

### Four levers against creative barriers

**Generativity** counters the blank canvas. A generated cast or map shrinks a huge possibility space down to small things the player wants to fix or change. It also eases fear of judgment, because players can disclaim the parts they dislike ("the game did that, not me") while claiming the parts they like ([Max Kreminski 2019, 7:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=461)).

**Incrementality** counters writer's block. Kreminski cites Raymond Chandler's adage about having a man come through the door with a gun: keep introducing disruptive new elements so the story moves even when the player does not know what happens next. Recurring elf raiding parties in Dwarf Fortress and each year's draft of newly generated players in Football Manager do this ([Max Kreminski 2019, 8:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=486)).

**Boundedness** counters perfectionism. Restricting rerolls and undo forces players to live with mistakes and justify them narratively, which often makes better stories. In the Pro Vercelli Football Manager story, the player fat-fingered a UI decision and traded away a star player at a crucial moment, something the character would never do, and had to explain it in the story ([Max Kreminski 2019, 9:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=546)). By the same logic, permadeath works as a boundedness lever.

**Limited options** counter paralysis. Counter-intuitively for a creative tool, restricting what the player can do at any moment helps when they are enjoying the process rather than aiming at a specific result. Giving the system more agency moves creative burden onto it, so players can focus on the parts they care about while the system smooths over the rest ([Max Kreminski 2019, 9:51](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=591)).

Kreminski's Cozy Mystery Construction Kit shows the last two in an actual tool. It turns the open question "what should happen next?" into a choice among about five to seven generated actions: things a character might plausibly want, actions that advance an author-level goal, or revenge for an earlier action; five to seven alternatives worked well in testing ([Max Kreminski 2019, 21:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1266)). Every action is auto-described into a transcript that players can edit collaboratively, Google Docs style, or leave alone, so they get a written story without extra tracking and can exert as little creative agency as they like ([Max Kreminski 2019, 20:18](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1218)).

### Ownership through remembered choices

Players own a story when the game remembers what they did. Aaron A. Reed's Hollywood Visionary has the player make a movie, choosing genre, actors, colour or black and white, soundtrack and editing tightness, and these choices return later, from throwaway background descriptions to the villain citing your editing as subversive. Players email Reed about the movie they made: if enough small choices accumulate and the game calls them back in surprising ways, the result feels unique ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 8:02](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=482)). Lazer-Walker found the same with Computational Flaneur: a generated moment driven by the player's own input, even if all they did was stand at some GPS coordinates, feels like theirs in a way a funny bot tweet does not ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 20:23](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1223)).

> If enough choices build up over time and the game remembers they can adhere to something that feels unique. — [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 8:02](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=482)

### Places to reflect and write

Several speakers argue that meaning forms after play, and that the designer can make room for it. Cole Wehrle says games need places of reflection after play to generate meaning. His board game Oath has no written narrative, character advancement or named protagonists, and like a roguelike, how a player won matters more than who won; it generates its meaning in the post-game report ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 3:34](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=214)). Oath deliberately offers no in-game view of the past and instead ships a journal, because Wehrle wanted players to do the work of history-writing outside play rather than gamify it. Players drew comics, kept per-player records, wrote as a jilted historian, made a cookbook from the food cards and wrote fold-out poetry ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 25:47](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1547)).

A video game version of this came up at the 2018 lightning talks. A speaker who runs lethal old-school tabletop games proposed that when a roguelike says you have died, it could ask "would you like to describe your death?" and store a short player-written blurb in the high score list or morgue file. Frequent death has to be made special, and a terse "killed by an orc" becomes meaningful once described; letting the player write it also relieves the game of generating zany descriptions, as it eases the GM's job at the table ([Various 2018, 25:00](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1500)).

### Repair, assembly and reading

Some games are built so players repair a story from pieces. Grinblat cites Kreminski's term *extrapolative narrativization* and a paper by Kreminski, narrative designer Kate Manning and himself extending it to *reparative play*: games that provide only pre-narrative parts in disrepair, which players repair into an emergent narrative, ornamenting their run with details the game never represents ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 16:09](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=969)). Reed's 18 Cadence makes assembly the whole game: players move through a house that exists from 1800 to 2000 and drag fragments onto a workbench to compose and share stories, from a disgruntled housewife oppressed by the house to an ashtray smoking the last cigarette. Reed counts it a success because players made stories he had never thought of, and sums it up as telling stories with players, not at them ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 11:07](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=667)). Jamie Brittain holds up Kruggsmash's Dwarf Fortress videos as proof that extracting stories from Legends mode is a genuine creative act, collaborative creation that honours both the world's chaos and the creator's input ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 26:44](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1604)).

Jasmine Otto models her Druid Game on tarot, where the player is both querent and reader, stacking a deck of story elements to steer their own reading. The surprises come from cards that have many features, of which only a few get latched onto; such cards contain no AI and so cannot have bugs, yet still produce funny surprises ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 5:00](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=300)). She separates *verbs*, which change world state, from *storylets*, prose with no game consequences that exist only in the reader's mind, where the sense of interaction is ultimately created; finding the boundary between them is a core design question for her ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 11:27](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=687)).

Other co-creative tools hand players authorial power more directly. Courtney Liessen's Reality Break experiments with letting players rewrite what NPCs say, with the change rippling into reality, like a conversation tree where you choose the other person's line. A generic rewrite system made a first version easy, but she says fully realising it could be its own game, and it raises questions about rewriting what someone said just to get a better item ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 17:35](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=1055)). Martin Pichlmair traces map-drawing games like The Quiet Year, where making the map together is the main gameplay, to an old tradition of rhetorical maps, from fantasy utopias to maps of Dante's hell, that show what places mean rather than where they are ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 19:10](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1150)). Whose story is it then? Grinblat, generating text from a corpus he largely wrote himself, adopts Emily Short's description of writing with a generator as a collaboration between author and generator ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 13:26](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=806)).

### The theatre model

Nic Junius, a former playwright, offers theatre as an analogue. He calls theatre a human-powered story generator: the script supplies constraints, and each production generates an always-different finished work, which is why Shakespeare and Greek tragedy are still retold ([Nic Junius 2023, 6:51](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=411)). There is never a single universal version of a script; the production is what finishes it, and productions differ even in the same year with the same people ([Nic Junius 2023, 5:20](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=320)). Two productions of Macbeth with identical words can make Macbeth either manipulated by the witches and Lady Macbeth or the one driving events, depending on small choices such as whether the witches touch him and whether he notices ([Nic Junius 2023, 9:02](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=542)). So even a linear scene with few choices can contain play, as players find new things in fixed game levels ([Nic Junius 2023, 8:14](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=494)). Players return to roguelikes and to plays for the same reason: to find something new in the familiar and explore as much of the story's volume as they can ([Nic Junius 2023, 15:17](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=917)). Junius has read Hades' run progression as a theatrical production, from a bad cold read through rehearsal-like practice to an "opening night" when the credits roll, and says playwriting taught him to bound a story's possibility space and let the production fill the gaps rather than branch ([Nic Junius 2024, 6:16](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=376)). In this model the player's run is the production, and your authored content is the script it finishes.

**In practice:** levers a designer can pull to make players better storytellers:

- Start them with a generated situation to react to, not a blank page ([Max Kreminski 2019, 7:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=461)).
- Keep introducing disruptions so the story never stalls ([Max Kreminski 2019, 8:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=486)).
- Limit undo and rerolls so mistakes become plot ([Max Kreminski 2019, 9:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=546)).
- Offer a small menu of plausible next events rather than open-ended freedom ([Max Kreminski 2019, 9:51](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=591); [Max Kreminski 2019, 21:06](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1266)).
- Remember small choices and call them back ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 8:02](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=482)).
- Give a place to write it down: an editable transcript, a journal, a player-written death note ([Max Kreminski 2019, 20:18](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1218); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 25:47](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1547); [Various 2018, 25:00](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1500)).
- Ship parts that need repairing and fragments that need assembling, rather than finished arcs ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 16:09](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=969); [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 11:07](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=667)).

## Story shapes that fit a roguelike

Not every narrative form survives permadeath and repetition. The talks point to a set of shapes that fit the genre's grain, and to some that work against it.

### Short stories, picaresques and rogues

Michael Brough traces the roguelike to fantasy fiction and argues short adventure stories suit it better than epic trilogies. The early twentieth-century pulp magazines were an accessible market for short stories, much like the later Flash games market, and short stories tell brief, self-contained arcs of discovery, adventure, success and failure; novels and epic trilogies have epic heroes, short stories have rogues ([Michael Brough 2025, 14:02](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=842)). The same shape carried into tabletop play: each D&D session needs its own satisfying self-contained arc, even within a longer campaign, or people will not keep coming back weekly, and pulp short stories modelled that structure ([Michael Brough 2025, 16:03](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=963)). Brough calls the *picaresque*, a form dating to the sixteenth century about a down-on-their-luck character surviving by wits whose successes are temporary and often lost, essentially the roguelike novel. Jack Vance's Cugel stories are highly episodic: occasionally Cugel carries money or items into the next chapter, but often he meets disaster and enters it with nothing ([Michael Brough 2025, 37:27](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2247)). Cugel gains a powerful magic item, such as boot polish that makes kicked things fly, and loses it through his own over-ambition, yet earns grudging admiration by getting up after each knockback ([Michael Brough 2025, 39:35](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2375)).

The protagonist's motive matters. Darren Grey contrasts the hero (noble cause, defender of the establishment, destined) with the rogue (self-interest, rebel, accidentally involved), and argues destiny clashes with the genre: you cannot be the one true chosen one when you are the 1048th player killed this month ([Darren Grey 2020, 15:43](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=943)). He links this to presentation: if artwork and names emphasise a heroic warrior, players approach permadeath like a standard RPG and do not behave as the game needs, and he traces much of reviewers' frustration with permadeath to that framing. A theme that emphasises threat, danger and trickiness tells players they are playing a rogue ([Darren Grey 2020, 17:38](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1058)). During a NetHack speedrun, a commentator relayed the description of the typical roguelike character as a "murder hobo" who kills, steals and wears random clothes, behaviour the game normalises ([Adeon 2017, 1:23:19](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=4999)).

### Stories about systems, not chosen ones

Sherveen Uduwana argues roguelikes suit a kind of story games often struggle with: stories about systemic change, societies and moments in time rather than single individuals, because the genre's own elements do much of the heavy lifting ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 2:24](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=144)). Repetition helps. Borrowing from music theory, he notes that a "wrong" jazz note repeated several times starts to sound intentional; the cyclical repetition of roguelikes legitimises narrative risks that would read as mistakes in other genres ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 5:02](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=302)). He lists what the run structure makes possible:

- **Failure without dissonance.** Linear games often have you play a sequence well and then show a cutscene of the character failing. Because roguelike players expect failure, characters can fail in the story without that dissonance, allowing more complex narratives with failure in them ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 7:35](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=455)).
- **Rotating protagonists.** The genre does not need a single protagonist. A roguelike set in revolutionary France could vary characters across runs so that social class shapes events, exploring the ideas of Les Misérables rather than being an action game in period costume ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 6:21](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=381)).
- **Vignettes.** Less reliance on one linear run lets a game tell a story through disparate vignettes on unrelated ideas, as the film Andrei Rublev does, while keeping an overall context; he points to Cultist Simulator, Outer Wilds and Rain World as games whose experience varies greatly with how you engage their systems ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 9:46](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=586)).
- **Unreliable narrators.** Repeated runs could let players experience a Rashomon-like story and gradually distil what is objective. The Stanley Parable and Her Story explore similar ideas, but Uduwana has found no roguelike that clearly does this and does not see why the genre is not full of them ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 11:13](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=673)). This is an open opportunity.

### Against prescriptive structure, for the power fantasy

Jamie Brittain argues that story-structure manuals like the hero's journey and Save the Cat are fine as descriptive tools, and most writers use them, but become harmful when executives and commissioners turn them into prescriptions; the result is a "narrative predictability crisis" in which audiences can tell when it is safe to leave a film for the toilet ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 9:05](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=545)). He links this to Brian Walker's 2016 warning that the biggest risk to a game's longevity is challenge becoming rote and systematised: screenwriting manuals kill the friction of film and TV the same way ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 10:31](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=631)). Story structures also favour happy endings, the hero returning with the elixir, while some of the best narrative experiences lack them. A roguelike's indifference to whether you live or die, even on NetHack's first level, is a narrative strength ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 19:54](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1194)). Andrew Cedotal adds a thematic objection: the hero's journey dramatises resisting off-ramps on a single path, which made sense when people accepted common virtues and worked hard at them. Today's core anxiety, he argues, is an overwhelming number of superficially viable options, and work that speaks to modern people should evoke and relieve that anxiety ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 25:13](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1513)).

Yet Brittain does not throw out the hero. His first lesson is that structure is a tool, not a prescription, and that the power fantasy is worth keeping: an overpowered Binding of Isaac run feels like nothing else. A winning NetHack run is an exquisite hero's journey by design (descend, retrieve, ascend), even though most players in actual play feel anything but heroic ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 11:55](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=715)). That tension between designed arc and lived experience is something to use, not resolve.

### How much overarching structure?

The talks split on whether a roguelike needs a shaped arc above the run. Tarn Adams found Dwarf Fortress's adventure mode flat: an open world of towns, monsters and bandits with no overarching structure, where players often just die or amuse themselves being bards. Traditional roguelikes, by contrast, get a quest-like structure from going deeper through generated levels ([Tarn Adams 2018, 1:25](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=85)). His fix was villains whose schemes map naturally onto plot and act structure: a villain who interlocks with a townsperson who talks to someone else to start a ball rolling has the same structure as the stories players already tell about items, terrain and a monster pushing them into it ([Tarn Adams 2018, 5:59](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=359)). He describes different opposition models for emergent narrative: Shadow of Mordor has the player fight through a generated organisational hierarchy within RPG-like plot arcs, while Pirates!-style games make the player a small cog in a strategy game that runs without them; he wants all of these at once ([Tarn Adams 2018, 8:25](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=505)). Matt Carney names the simplest structure a roguelike has: its *pulse*, a clear, linear sense of motion and purpose such as descending a dungeon or climbing a tower, around which any weird generated content can cohere. Even a set map like Caves of Qud's yields different linear paths each time ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1378)).

Others gave up on shaped endings. Emilia Lazer-Walker tried emulating the culminating structures of Sleep No More, roguelike deaths and Dear Esther for Computational Flaneur, using music to shape emotion and detecting waning attention to wrap up, but these proved more trouble than they were worth. The design instead followed a Twitter-bot model that works whether you walk for five minutes or five hours ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:19](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=979)). Cole Wehrle describes two approaches in his own work: Arcs is built as a three-act story, while Oath cannot have a beginning, middle and end and relies on remembering, forgetting and assembling stories afterwards ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 31:13](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1873)).

Tim Keenan's experience is a caution against going too far. Duskers deliberately closed each storyline without bringing them all to one final resolution, because he felt that would end the game and work against the roguelike structure. He stands by the choice, but players strongly wanted a definitive ending, and he would consider adding one next time ([Tim Keenan 2017, 12:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=734)).

The choice depends on length and on what holds the run together. A run with a strong pulse already has a spine ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1378)); an open world without one, like Adams' adventure mode, feels flat ([Tarn Adams 2018, 1:25](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=85)); an experience of unpredictable length may be better without a climax at all ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:19](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=979)); and players who have invested in several storylines may still want an ending ([Tim Keenan 2017, 12:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=734)).

**In practice:** choosing a shape:

- If runs are short and death is frequent, think in short stories and picaresque episodes: self-contained arcs, gains that are temporary ([Michael Brough 2025, 14:02](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=842); [Michael Brough 2025, 37:27](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2247)).
- Frame the protagonist as a rogue acting from self-interest, and let theme and art signal danger rather than destiny ([Darren Grey 2020, 15:43](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=943); [Darren Grey 2020, 17:38](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1058)).
- Consider telling the story of a society or system across rotating protagonists, vignettes or unreliable accounts ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 2:24](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=144); [Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 6:21](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=381); [Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 11:13](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=673)).
- Make sure the run has a pulse; if it does not, give the world agents with schemes that supply plot ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1378); [Tarn Adams 2018, 5:59](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=359)).
- Decide deliberately whether there is an ending, and expect invested players to want one ([Tim Keenan 2017, 12:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=734)).

## Death, restarts and the loop as narrative

Every narrative roguelike must decide what death and restarting mean in its fiction. For a long time the answer was nothing. Marc Dolgin notes that early roguelikes gave no in-world reason for restarting because that was simply how the mechanics worked; increasingly, especially in response to Hades, games like Hades and Cobalt Core build the restart into their lore, which raises the importance of lore and immersion in roguelites ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 30:54](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1854)).

### Whether to justify the restart

Harry Solomons calls the restart a mechanic that started as a technical limitation but is an immensely powerful narrative tool. Hades frames the same character returning with the same memories, which mirrors the player's own experience; leaving restarts unexplained, on the other hand, invites players to draw their own conclusions ([Harry Solomons 2024, 24:30](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1470)). Dolgin ties the choice to tone: in comedic roguelikes players do not worry about lore, but once a game becomes more serious, players want to be immersed and start asking why they are starting over ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 35:14](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2114)). Tim Keenan found that showing the intro once and pretending the character remembers did not go far enough for Duskers ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224)); instead, he framed the protagonist as the actual player at the keyboard, using sci-fi multiverse framing, so discovered logs persist across deaths while the gameplay challenge stays the same every run ([Tim Keenan 2017, 4:33](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=273)).

So the decision runs roughly like this: a light or comic tone can skip justification; a serious tone creates an expectation of one; an unexplained restart is itself a legitimate choice that hands interpretation to the player.

### The costs of story under repetition

Authored story strains under the loop. Keenan names repetition as the first problem curated narrative has in roguelikes: a long intro cutscene you sit through every run would obviously be a burden ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224)). Andrew Aversa makes the same point: a permadeath game cannot front-load an intrusive, JRPG-style cinematic opening, because replaying the early game makes even the best opening stale very quickly ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:46](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=826)).

Rich Wilson treats the deeper problem as unsolved. Reconciling a replayable system with a dramatic story is still an open question; Prey: Mooncrash handled it with a frame narrative in which the player is a hacker on an isolated satellite running a simulation of a moon base, so the static story was told outside while the loops ran safely inside ([Rich Wilson 2021, 21:12](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1272)). The related problem of drama versus agency, keeping the player from breaking a carefully planned narrative, is also unsolved; Mooncrash sidestepped it by keeping its handcrafted beats as character threads that wove orthogonally through play and could not be failed ([Rich Wilson 2021, 22:06](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1326)).

Attachment cuts both ways. Lisa Brown became so attached to her character in Road Not Taken, an emotional story about its creator's decision not to have children, that her first permadeath was traumatising and she never played again. She notes that for her low-immersion profile, narrative is mostly a wrapper, and players who want high immersion might love such a game ([Lisa Brown 2020, 22:14](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1334)). Stella Vermilion's Nuzlocke runs, described among the raw ingredients of emergent story, show the other side: there loss is what builds the attachment to nicknamed party members ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:56:18](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32178)). The difference seems to be whether loss is part of the expected shape of play or a blow against a story the player was invested in.

### Hauntology: the ghosts of failed runs

Solomons gives the most developed account of death as theme. He borrows *hauntology*: media with a paradoxical relationship to time, an eeriness of things wrongly present or absent, and places stained by traces of past events. Through Mark Fisher, eeriness is either a failure of absence (something present that should not be) or a failure of presence (something missing that should be there) ([Harry Solomons 2024, 7:08](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=428)). His thesis is that roguelikes are inherently hauntological, because permadeath forces players to retread and trample over the ghosts of their own failed runs ([Harry Solomons 2024, 10:19](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=619)).

Two games make this explicit. When Inscryption defeats you, it invites you to compose a *death card* from attributes of your failed deck, write your name on it, and have your photo taken; you later draw that card, pull yourself out of the deck and sacrifice yourself ([Harry Solomons 2024, 2:03](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=123)). In Returnal, Selene knows she is looping, finds her own corpses carrying notes she does not remember, and those corpses can reanimate and kill her. Each corpse is a version of you that failed, a lost successful future that stains the space you must cross ([Harry Solomons 2024, 12:29](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=749)).

> Each corpse represents a version of you that failed. A potential successful future that never came to pass. — [Harry Solomons 2024, 12:29](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=749)

Solomons asks designers to engage with what death means in their worlds: the genre lets you write death over and over on top of itself, so places can become stained by repeated failure and the loop becomes something to confront ([Harry Solomons 2024, 13:32](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=812)). Time-loop stories offer a power fantasy that enough retries and information can prevent tragedy, and he ties their popularity to doomscrolling and anxiety; games that take that fantasy away can powerfully reframe the present ([Harry Solomons 2024, 14:50](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=890)). His closing request is to consider how failure loops imprint on the places players move through, and what is gained by withholding the power fantasy, as Inscryption and especially Returnal do ([Harry Solomons 2024, 18:10](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1090)). Even winning has to be handled: restarting after a victory can undercut the theme unless it is deliberate, as when Inscryption's perfect win drags you back into the same chair ([Harry Solomons 2024, 23:04](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1384)). In Q&A he agreed with an audience suggestion that reloading a save can feel like possessing a past self; the host, Alexei, added the eeriness of decision-heavy games where you remember a timeline in which you got someone killed ([Harry Solomons 2024, 20:55](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1255)).

The loop can also carry a gentler theme. Dolgin describes The Void Rains Upon Her Heart, whose story is built around having to start over whether you win or lose, as reflecting real-life struggles with anxiety and depression: starting over is framed as part of life, the way people move on and get better ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 32:32](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1952)).

### The persistence toolkit

Between "nothing persists" and full metaprogression lies a range of tools that carry story, not power, across deaths. Jim Shepard calls this *meta presence*: world elements that respond to the player's past runs without changing gameplay difficulty. It suits purists who do not want power carryover, and it tells a repeatedly dying player that the things she does matter ([Jim Shepard 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=818)). His example is Caves of Qud's Joppa: after one character solves the water-well quest, the next hears the same quest from scratch. A meta-presence version would have the mayor acknowledge what past characters discovered, the same place and the same monsters, as a nod to the player; that makes the world less static, which is a design choice, but does not change the gameplay ([Jim Shepard 2017, 16:03](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=963)). Other ideas include tavern drinks named after past heroes, town tributes, a barkeep who remembers a hero who saved his son, or an NPC related to a previous character whose gameplay job stays the same; he cautions that player-chosen names can break a world's theme ([Jim Shepard 2017, 17:06](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1026)). Dungeonmans goes further: when a hero dies, a dungeon appears with the killer as its boss. Shepard admits it is "kind of broken", since a scrappy level-2 monster that landed the last hit becomes king over stronger ones, but it makes the game feel like a campaign that rises and falls with its heroes ([Jim Shepard 2017, 18:10](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1090)). Thomas Biskup said ADOM's team was considering a similar idea, with a monster that killed your ADOM character resurfacing in Ultimate ADOM as a named nemesis, citing Shadow of Mordor as a model ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 32:54](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1974)).

Shepard's broader claim is that metaprogression is really a set of storytelling tools: players do not recount every dull death, they tie their runs into highlight-reel stories that they tell each other, a meta story across many runs ([Jim Shepard 2017, 19:18](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1158)).

Lineage is another option. Darkest Dungeon treats successive characters as recruits, and a host on the Rise of the Roguelite panel suggested framing permadead characters as generations, so players think in lineages and see many perspectives rather than playing an anonymous @ to be forgotten ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 39:55](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2395)). Uduwana cites The Swindle, where a failed heist costs you your character and gives you a new one, Rogue Legacy's descendants with unique quirks, and Wildermyth, where a character's personality colours how similar events play out ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 7:48](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=468)).

### Death screens, messages and chronologies

The moment of death is itself a storytelling surface. Zach and Tarn Adams describe Dwarf Fortress's Legends mode as a high score list, a shared memory of exploits descended from the one-line death sentence with a killer's name and date in Hack and NetHack; that sentence was the seed of their whole narrative approach ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 18:08](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=1088)). At the 2018 lightning talks Kawa pointed out that the death screen immediately tells the player what kind of game they played: Dungeons of Dredmor's ornate "congratulations, you have died" is jokey and trope-mocking, while Caves of Qud reports who killed you, their faction and their beliefs, conveying that you were one mutant among many in a living world ([Various 2018, 12:33](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=753)). Specificity is what makes a death message tell a story: a barbarian who "choked on his own vomit while paralyzed" can be visualised without further explanation, unlike "killed by an orc" ([Various 2018, 24:03](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1443)). Qud's death screen also includes a chronology that retells the character's life as a list of story events, from quests and discoveries to recruited followers and the killer ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 58:02](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=3482)). The player-written death blurb described under "Players as co-authors" is the participatory version of the same idea ([Various 2018, 25:00](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1500)).

**In practice:** options for making death meaningful in the fiction:

- Decide whether the restart needs an in-world reason; match the decision to your tone ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 35:14](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2114); [Harry Solomons 2024, 24:30](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1470)).
- Keep anything that replays every run short, and move story out of the opening ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:46](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=826)).
- Persist knowledge and lore across deaths even if power does not persist ([Tim Keenan 2017, 4:33](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=273)).
- Let failed runs leave traces in the world: corpses, cards, nemeses, NPCs who remember ([Harry Solomons 2024, 2:03](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=123); [Harry Solomons 2024, 12:29](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=749); [Jim Shepard 2017, 18:10](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1090); [Jim Shepard 2017, 16:03](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=963)).
- Frame successive characters as a lineage or rotating cast ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 39:55](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2395); [Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 7:48](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=468)).
- Make the death screen specific: who, why, and a chronology of the life ([Various 2018, 12:33](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=753); [Various 2018, 24:03](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1443); [Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 58:02](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=3482)).
- Decide what the loop means thematically, including what happens after a win ([Harry Solomons 2024, 13:32](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=812); [Harry Solomons 2024, 23:04](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1384)).

## When fiction and mechanics pull together

The sections so far are about the stories players make. The next five turn to the world the designer builds for them to make stories in: its rules, its numbers, its tone, its setting and its words. The first requirement is that the fiction and the rules agree. Tim Keenan argues that curated story in roguelikes is disliked mainly not because it exists but because it sits beside the game instead of inside it. Reflecting on Duskers, he puts the problem in one image: fish escaping a net only get out if they all swim the same way. A curated story that pulls in its own direction does nothing for the game or actively works against it, and he admits Duskers did not fully manage this ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:23](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=203)). The term the talks use for the failure is *ludonarrative dissonance*: what the story says and what the rules make you do disagree.

### Make the player live the story, not hear about it

Two talks arrive at the same remedy from different directions. Jongwoo Kim calls Kitfox's approach in The Shrouded Isle *subjective simulation*: model a community's psychological reality and values rather than its objective material conditions, so the narrative is told through the decisions the player makes. Kim finds this more impactful than scripted content or walls of text because the player takes part in each decision and is personally responsible for what follows ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 3:57](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=237)). Jim Shepard makes the same argument at the level of a single scene. A fight in a burning village beats a text box from a survivor describing the fire, and it costs nothing extra:

> Don't make a puppy cave, make a town on fire. — [Jim Shepard 2018, 9:26](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=566)

The monsters are just as easy and the tutorial steps the same, but theme and story arrive for free ([Jim Shepard 2018, 9:26](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=566)). Sherveen Uduwana adds why this works especially well in games: players are forced to build a conscious mental model of the system in order to experience the narrative, and that modelling is itself material a designer can tell stories with ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 2:59](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=179)).

The Shrouded Isle shows how deep the alignment can go. The cult's values are the game's resources, so even a player who dislikes promoting ignorance has to keep the town ignorant to succeed. Because those resources are dissociated from the villagers' wellbeing, the player's interests split from the villagers' interests, and players willingly make Machiavellian choices ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 9:19](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=559)). The fiction is not explaining the mechanic; the mechanic is the fiction. The same structure turns resource accounting into drama. Kim appointed an advisor, Chesa, expecting her to raise ignorance; she lowered it, and her vice drained obedience. Because he had chosen and instructed her, he felt betrayed rather than self-blaming; with a pure process, he says, he would only have blamed himself ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 15:31](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=931)).

Shepard also points out that a procedurally generated roguelike still has acts and phases, its dungeon levels, and you can use those progression markers to change the hero. His example is a corruption meter: once it crosses a threshold, the hero answers the same shopkeeper differently, so the player experiences the arc while playing. Keep important information on the critical path and let fluff support it ([Jim Shepard 2018, 28:53](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1733)).

### A thin layer of fiction can sell a mechanic

The cheapest version of integration is a fiction that makes an existing rule feel right. Several developers describe the same surprise at how little it takes:

- **Against the Storm.** The early Queen's Impatience was a bare 30-60 minute timer that the developers call one of the worst mechanics in their demo. Dressing it as a visible, impatient queen made players accept it and react to it emotionally; a streamer screamed "please" at her. The developer was stunned how much a thin layer of fiction that matches expectations achieved ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 26:53](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1613)).
- **Party House (UFO 50).** Jon Perry concedes the temporary ban after a bust is mechanically a bit clunky (a permanent ban would be too strong), but the story of kicking out the guilty guest sells it and gives frustrated players a character to blame instead of the developer ([Jon Perry 2025, 28:21](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1701)).
- **Pacific Drive.** Paul Dean explained the game's ubiquitous gasoline by making portable fuel essential in a world whose infrastructure keeps breaking down. He compares the job to writing for a collaborative tabletop sourcebook: describe existing elements in supporting ways, then fill in ordinary lives around them ([Paul Dean 2025, 10:05](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=605)).
- **Planet Zoldath (UFO 50).** Perry designed it role-playing as a fictional developer who had just discovered procgen, so wild, unbalanced seeds fit the game's place in UFO 50's meta-story, as long as every seed stayed solvable ([Jon Perry 2025, 32:56](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1976)).
- **Test Tube Titans.** Gabriel Koenig handles the uncomfortable feel of monster breeding through narrative: each titan decomposes after use, and the story is critical of the lab's monster-making. Asked about it, he notes that setting strongly shapes how such a mechanic feels ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 23:43](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=1423)).

### Mechanics that generate the story

The arrow can point the other way, with a mechanical decision producing the fiction. Eric Billingsley cut stairs from Into Ruins early, and the cut cascaded: the game now opens with the player drawn down into a chasm, and the goal item, the Wings of Yendor, is the only way back up. With stairs, he says, it would have been a completely different game ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 28:29](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1709)). In Caves of Qud, Ivy Melinda relays Caelyn Sandel's account of how the mopango grew from a character build into a settled culture: their subterranean nature fit a settlement in a cramped tomb, and Quaker-like traits gave them their pseudospeech, a small narrative leap from build to concept ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 17:48](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=1068)).

Michael Brough traces how a constraint creates a story shape. Vancian memorised magic exists so that the adventurer packs a few items and then solves each challenge by applying one of them, sometimes creatively, the structure of fairy tales and James Bond gadget setups. Without some limit on a wizard's power, stories about wizards are hard to tell; Gandalf being conveniently absent is another fix for the same problem ([Michael Brough 2025, 28:43](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=1723)).

Emotion can be the starting point too. The Banished Vault was designed around three target emotions, size, hostility and unpredictability, which the player should feel imposed on them and then overcome; Nic Tringali calls overcoming them the positive feeling the designers wanted ([Nic Tringali 2023, 5:12](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=312)). Its exploration is modelled on real space exploration, an unknown journey toward a relatively known goal, like knowing an oasis exists without knowing the way there ([Nic Tringali 2023, 11:58](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=718)).

Nic Junius argues that tying story progress to non-narrative systems such as combat makes everything feel like it matters to the narrative, even systems that rarely talk to each other, and steers players toward the story rather than pure optimisation ([Nic Junius 2024, 31:31](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1891)). Spencer Egart's procedural rituals do the same for reading: ritual instructions are scattered through in-game books and dialogue, so players read world text because it has mechanical value, which he cheerfully calls tricking people into reading ([Spencer Egart 2019, 13:17](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=797)). Keenan's Duskers ties story objectives to procedurally placed elements, so the same written story plays differently: in one run you find the research station first and hunt for an old ship, in another you find the ship first and must cruise around in a poorly suited vessel looking for a station ([Tim Keenan 2017, 7:07](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=427)).

### Where it goes wrong

Mechanics that speak loudly can also say things players never hear. Jeff Lait's experiments with long-term consequences are the clearest cautionary set. In Vicious Orcs, free-mana spellcasting made the game trivially easy (teleport back, heal, repeat) while freezing fields and sickening villagers, and the good ending required avoiding it. Lait hoped the sudden drop in difficulty would read as a warning, but he believes no player found that ending on their own ([Jeff Lait 2025, 19:15](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1155)). A later 7DRL made the consequence overt: casting spells progressively strips item descriptions to bare utility, so an elegant sword becomes a source of wood, and the ending depends on how decayed your world view is; finishing without spells gives the best ending ([Jeff Lait 2025, 20:25](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1225)). In Sword in Hand, where the player is a sword choosing war or peace missions, the ending is scored by how long the world takes to repopulate, and Lait deliberately leaves open whose good ending counts: the sword's, the people's, the king's or the player's ([Jeff Lait 2025, 22:29](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1349)). The lesson from the first case is that a signal hidden in the difficulty curve may simply go unread; the later games put the consequence where players look.

Nathan Savant warns about the most intimate mechanical lever. Changing moment-to-moment input to express a character's inner struggle, as The Last of Us does when Ellie doesn't respond, or making a character unable to focus or to tell friend from foe in anger, is powerful but "very touchy": most of the time, altering movement speed or input response is about the worst thing you can do to a player ([Nathan Savant 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=658)).

Simulation can also contradict the prose without anyone choosing it. Ivy Melinda points out that Caves of Qud's 1,200-turn day implies either 72-second turns or two-hour days; simulated and handwritten narratives collide, sometimes hilariously, and the player has to suspend disbelief ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 7:04](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=424)).

### Optional, but load-bearing

If integration is the goal, how central should authored story be? Keenan defends curated narrative on the same grounds as in any game: it supplies mid- and long-term goals, mystery and a compelling question, such as Duskers' "why is everybody dead?", which some players only start asking 10 or 20 hours in ([Tim Keenan 2017, 1:48](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=108)). Yet he also made it optional: players can ignore the logs, while those who read about a military conspiracy might beeline for the next military ship, letting story discoveries shape strategy ([Tim Keenan 2017, 15:30](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=930)). To avoid a single story goal that players fixate on, Duskers offers several optional branching storylines, essentially achievements built into the story, each needing particular upgrades or conditions; depending on what a run contains, a different storyline becomes the lucky opportunity ([Tim Keenan 2017, 10:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=614)). Tabea Iseli's team on Grimoire Groves feared that the dialogue needed to explain its non-violent mechanics would turn players off; instead players asked for more story, and the team leaned in partly because narrative helps newcomers understand how roguelikes work ([Tabea Iseli 2024, 6:54](https://youtu.be/-MX1imoSxTg?t=414)).

**In practice**, check each mechanic against its fiction:

- Does the rule make the player *do* what the story is about, or only *watch* it? If a survivor could describe it, consider making it a fight or a decision ([Jim Shepard 2018, 9:26](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=566)).
- If a rule feels arbitrary, is there a character or in-world cause that could own it, and give players someone other than you to blame ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 26:53](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1613); [Jon Perry 2025, 28:21](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1701))?
- Do your resources encode the values of the people in your fiction, so that succeeding means adopting their view ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 9:19](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=559))?
- If a consequence matters to the ending, will players actually notice the signal, or will they miss it ([Jeff Lait 2025, 19:15](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1155))?
- Can a player ignore the story and still play, and does a player who follows it get goals and strategy out of it ([Tim Keenan 2017, 15:30](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=930))?

## What your systems say about your world

Writers tend to think the world lives in the text. Xalavier Nelson Jr. came away from Space Warlord Organ Trading Simulator convinced of the opposite:
