> The generation systems, the statistics, the base numbers that build up this reality said more about our fictional world than the writing and marketing ever might. — [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 18:44](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1124)

Players experience the little integers far more often than they read your prose, and they read those integers as facts about the world.

### Every number is a claim

Nelson's examples show how quickly a technical choice becomes a worldview. Nelson spent 48 hours deciding what counts as an organ: nerves, teeth, eardrums. Skin is an organ, which raises whether selling it is acceptable and opens the possibility of valuing skin tones differently, a choice Nelson calls deeply messed up and a glimpse of real cultural biases. An arbitrary decision on the developers' part would be read by players as objective truth about the game's reality ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=331)). When programmer Sam Chet asked whether the soul is a sellable organ, the question spiralled into who has souls, how their quality varies, where they are harvested and whether aliens have them; the team decided aliens do and that souls are inherently human. Nelson treats this as emblematic: one simple systemic decision brings a spiralling series of implications ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 7:48](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=468)).

The effect reaches outside the game. Nelson cites Simon Parkin's Eurogamer investigation into arms manufacturers and studios to argue that game design decisions can be and are advertising: Modern Warfare 2's Barrett .50 cal sold rifles, and Doom made the double-barrelled shotgun the standard power weapon decades on, so departing from that standard is itself a statement ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 20:43](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1243)). Your own perspective leaks in too. In Airport for Aliens Currently Run by Dogs, Nelson, having just aged out of his healthcare, made the clinic NPC's punchline "I'm a doctor, not a monster", because in a utopia charging for care would be absurd ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 25:50](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1550)). James Cartlidge generalises the point as *procedural rhetoric*: games convey ideas through their mechanics, including ideas nobody intended, so mechanics can be read for meaning the way films are ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 22:37](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1357)).

### Systems as a storytelling channel

If systems will speak anyway, you can make them speak on purpose. Robin Mendoza proposes prices as a storytelling device. Following Hayek, he treats prices as quantitative indices that compress and transmit complex information, like a hash where any change in world conditions changes the numbers, though without revealing whether supply or demand moved. A merchant outside a dungeon charging double for an amulet could mean superstition, a subsidy, deforestation the player caused, or a real threat ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 1:50](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=110)). He lists what prices can encode in a roguelike: resource distribution that varies between games, community beliefs and prejudices (markups by the player's class or race), politics and subsidies, cornered markets, and repercussions of the player's own actions ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 3:01](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=181)). Pathologic is his worked example: after the first day prices skyrocket, which tells the player that news of the plague has spread, and pushes them into bartering with groups that want different things, with per-district reputation shaping their daily route ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 5:12](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=312)). The approach commits you to worldbuilding, though. In Q&A, the host notes that pricing a dungeon starts with asking why a shopkeeper exists on level six and how its supply chain works; Mendoza agrees it is hard to know where that thread stops, and adds that prices suggest a more social world of interacting agents ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 13:46](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=826)).

Generated structures imply worlds as well. Dustin Freeman's interest in Civilization VI's shuffle mode, which randomises the tech tree's topology while keeping eras, is in what the dependencies imply: astrology depending on animal husbandry, or a "bronze world" where all high technology is built from bronze ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 7:51](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=471)). Mike Cook makes the complementary point for generated mechanics: doors work because everyone knows what a door is, but a generated rule leaves you unsure what to tell the player the thing is, so you often need a theme, such as potions, spells, ancient languages or experimental technology, that explains why an object's effect is unknown. He concedes, via his "rubber Santa" experiment, that sometimes ignoring theme is fine ([Mike Cook 2023, 24:47](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1487)). John Harris, back in 2016, predicted roguelikes would move toward behind-the-scenes, algorithmically generated stories that explain the dungeon and that a canny player can exploit, an approach he saw in Dwarf Fortress ([John Harris 2016, 20:02](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1202)).

### Abstraction and space as meaning

The presentation layer is a system too. Ray reads Caves of Qud's abstractions, its grid, ASCII or tile visuals and tabletop-style mechanics, as narrative devices that suggest a mythologised, bardically unreliable telling rather than literal events, so the sharper edges of the simulation become tall-tale hyperbole instead of limitations ([Ray 2025, 3:31](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=211)). In the same reading, the player character has their own history reinterpreted at the Tomb of the Eaters, a mechanical parallel that loops back into the game's themes of a distorted deep past ([Ray 2025, 10:46](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=646)). Linas Gabrielaitis reads dungeon depth through geology, where digging deeper means finding older things: descent through layers is a spatialisation of time ([Linas Gabrielaitis 2023, 4:21](https://youtu.be/jvZb9WoIHxo?t=261)).

**In practice**, audit your numbers the way you would proofread your prose:

- List what your stats, categories and generators treat as countable, sellable or valuable, and ask what a player would conclude about your world from that list alone ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=331); [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 18:44](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1124)).
- Follow each odd question ("is the soul an organ?") to its implications before players do ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 7:48](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=468)).
- Pick a system, such as prices or tech dependencies, to carry news about the world deliberately, and decide how much of the supporting world you are willing to build ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 1:50](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=110); [Robin Mendoza 2024, 13:46](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=826)).
- Give generated mechanics a theme that explains why they are unknown ([Mike Cook 2023, 24:47](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1487)).

## Setting a tone and holding it

Tone is what makes a thousand scattered lines of item text, death messages and dialogue feel like one game. It also does narrative work of its own: as the first section noted, Jim Shepard credits Dungeonmans' tone, not its almost nonexistent plot, with giving players a trellis for their own stories ([Jim Shepard 2016, 3:16](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=196)). The fullest method in the talks is Shepard's account of how he set and enforced that tone.

### Pick a target on a map of other works

Shepard plotted existing fiction on axes: comedy from serious to zany, how much heroism is valued, and how important lore and setting are. Game of Thrones and Warhammer sit at the serious end, Dungeons of Dredmor and Monty Python at the zany end, and at both extremes heroism carries little weight. On lore, Pac-Man needs none, Myst needs it to win, and Skyrim has a huge amount that players can ignore. He aimed at funny but not zany, with heroism mattering and lore less necessary than Skyrim's ([Jim Shepard 2016, 4:29](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=269)). The result, "lighthearted heroic adventure", then served as a razor for every line, with some of Robert E. Howard's pulpy, sometimes dark feel kept where it fit and text that was too serious cut. Not all text can be funny, so the question is not whether a line is funny:

> Does this work in the game, not necessarily is it funny, but does it work in the game. — [Jim Shepard 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=420)

### Deliver it in the background

Shepard ranks delivery methods. The worst is shoving humour in the player's face, which only works if you are very good at fully zany comedy; better is placing it along the critical path; best is making it a comfortable background, like a fire keeping you warm while you attend to your cup of "gameplay tea" ([Jim Shepard 2016, 8:13](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=493)). Paul Dean frames the same restraint as drumming: what you leave out and when matters as much as what you play, and the amount of writing should suit the game's tone and pace. Nuclear Throne's one-liners need no thunderous rock drummer, and in Pacific Drive the writing had to complement the rest of the team's work rather than ruin it ([Paul Dean 2025, 11:34](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=694)).

Once set, a tone is easy to break. Shepard warns against abruptly moving a funny game into dark drama to make the player "feel it", citing Borderlands 2's sudden character deaths: unless your audience wants that, it backfires and wastes the power of the target you set ([Jim Shepard 2016, 25:26](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1526)).

### Humour rules

Shepard's humour advice is conservative, by design:

- **References must be invisible to those who miss them.** "How many Bothans had to die" fails for players who haven't seen Star Wars, but "many scrollbulls died to bring this information" works because scrollbulls exist in Dungeonmans. A reference should read as an ordinary in-world fact and never be the main punchline ([Jim Shepard 2016, 18:25](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1105)).
- **Play to your strengths.** Take creative risks elsewhere but play it safe with humour. Shepard knew he could write funny dialogue, descriptions and objects, but not long-form humour or slapstick cutscenes, so he left those out ([Jim Shepard 2016, 22:42](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1362)).
- **Avoid edgy humour.** It alienates players and ages badly; he cites problematic material in Grand Theft Auto V, Predator and Robert E. Howard, and notes the audience is moving toward inclusiveness ([Jim Shepard 2016, 24:05](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1445)).
- **Study, target, playtest.** Watch, play and read funny things to learn what works for you, pick a target, and test jokes on friends, cutting what doesn't land; you QA humour like anything else ([Jim Shepard 2016, 27:20](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1640)).
- **Borrow a rhythm.** Dungeonmans' Psychomancer powers take the structure of karate tall tales, a thing happens, a thing happens, then a twist, chosen because the source's tone matched the target ([Jim Shepard 2016, 22:06](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1326)).

Generated text can be funny by construction. Zack Johnson explains that Kingdom of Loathing's guard names juxtapose an ordinary part with a silly one, a silly first name with a normal surname or the reverse, as in "Paul Blart"; the team's rule is that any person-name generator must be able to produce "Bob Goldwater", funny precisely because it is so ordinary ([Zack Johnson 2016, 15:14](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=914)). Topical humour is the risky kind. Jeff Olson's Alphaman built castles around pop-culture parodies with special mechanics, Grandpa Munster turning you into a bat and scattering your items, Gilligan breaking an item every turn, but he notes much of that topical humour has not survived the test of time ([Jeff Olson 2023, 15:00](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=900)), which is Shepard's ageing warning seen from the other side.

### Tone that grows, and tone that widens

Shepard's method fixes the tone up front. Blaseball shows a different path: Joel Clark says it did not start as a horror game, but players were intrigued by the forbidden book and the incinerations, so the team leaned into the weird and horror elements, while saying they would back off if the community's reaction became "this is too much" ([Joel Clark 2020, 25:24](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1524)). The choice depends on whether your game is a finished artefact or a live conversation with its players. And a tone target need not be narrow. Julian Day deliberately added limited poetic touches, such as Shadow of the Wyrm's wildflower descriptions, so the world would be about poetry and art as well as monsters and dungeons ([Julian Day 2020, 11:03](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=663)).

**In practice:** place three to six works you know on Shepard's axes, mark your target, and write a one-line tone statement ([Jim Shepard 2016, 4:29](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=269)). Run every line through it as a razor ([Jim Shepard 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=420)), put most of the tone in the background ([Jim Shepard 2016, 8:13](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=493)), write only the kinds of humour you are good at ([Jim Shepard 2016, 22:42](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1362)), and playtest jokes ([Jim Shepard 2016, 27:20](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1640)). If you change tone later, do it because your audience is asking for it ([Joel Clark 2020, 25:24](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1524); [Jim Shepard 2016, 25:26](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1526)).

## Choosing a setting and theme

Setting is often chosen last and treated as a skin. The talks treat it as a design lever: a theme supplies mechanics, holds generated content together, decides how much explaining you have to do, and can carry meaning through structure.

### Theme as a source of mechanics and coherence

Josh Ge argues that a unique non-fantasy theme is an underused hook: it makes the whole experience distinctive and gives you a source from which to draw new mechanics. Historical and mythological themes offer large bodies of material, sci-fi is in demand, and he cites MakaiRL (Japanese mythology), Skies of Bloody April (dogfighting) and Lone Spelunker, noting pirates and superheroes are often requested but rarely made ([Josh Ge 2018, 20:15](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1215)). Matt Carney explains why a shared setting matters for generation. Terry Riley's In C coheres because all its patterns share a key; generated content coheres when it shares a setting, theme or genre, a layer he calls "key and notes". In Rogue everything is "of the dungeon", a coherence of proximity, though Carney finds the Yetis slightly dissonant, and slight dissonance can be welcome ([Matt Carney 2026, 19:03](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1143)).

Familiar settings bring free understanding. Tyler Coleman observes that medieval fantasy easily gets you 80% familiarity from known tropes, even for magic, while a sci-fi item name means something different in every game. For Space Merchant he used "narrative greebles": keep a familiar base noun and attach a novel modifier, as in "tachyon disruptor rifle" ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 16:22](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=982)). Borrowing an entire existing world is the extreme case. Santiago Zapata describes Moria as the first XRL, a roguelike adapting an existing setting (here The Lord of the Rings); where Hack built its own world, Moria pioneered using Rogue's conventions as a shared language for adventures in many settings, and XRLs are now many players' entry point to the genre ([Santiago Zapata 2022, 10:38](https://youtu.be/y6WCq0jYbHo?t=638)).

### Believable, coherent worlds

Thomas Biskup started ADOM partly because NetHack's tourists and samurai clashed with his wish for a believable, story-coherent world, a matter of personal taste rather than a flaw in NetHack ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 1:41](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=101)). David Craddock reports that Biskup missed taking part in a story, since NetHack felt like a puzzle about optimising your way to the Amulet, and so balanced static authored elements with procedural ones: each adventure is new, but players feel part of a larger story ([David Craddock 2016, 14:58](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=898)). Ultimate ADOM extends that story rather than discarding it. One of ADOM's ultra endings, a champion's fight with the chaos lord, shatters Ancardia into a multiverse of similar but varied worlds that share rules, engine and monsters, which gives a story reason for multiple games and platform variants ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 10:31](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=631)). It adds seven factions with their own agendas in the law-versus-chaos conflict, each with minor benefits and hindrances, plus an unaligned option for players who just want to explore ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 7:01](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=421)). Biskup also admits ADOM never explained its backstory at the start in its first 25 years, so Ultimate ADOM opens with a trailer that establishes the lord of chaos, the cataclysm and the player as someone buried alive ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 5:10](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=310)).

Caves of Qud reaches coherence differently. Jason Grinblat describes its post-apocalyptic setting as drawing on Gamma World, but with the pre-fall past obscured by time and cultural mashups, so players cannot readily identify with it as they can in Fallout ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 1:47](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=107)). Its handcrafted RPG narrative is woven around simulation: physical systems where you can dig anywhere and every wall has a melting point, social systems of factions and reputation, and a history generated at the start of every game that seeds world generation ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 1:40](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=100)). Phillip Daigle offers the writer's test: lore should give rise to interesting gameplay scenarios and come from your own genuine interest, because lore written to please an imagined audience shows its insincerity; he favours lightweight lore that players fill in themselves ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 20:39](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1239)).

### Bounded and strange spaces

Roguelikes have always liked enclosed places, and Everest Pipkin explains why. Islands and other bordered settings give the designer a controllable space where the rules can differ: you build the edge of the world first, then a garden inside it ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 13:27](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=807)). Pipkin's own The Barnacle Goose Experiment seals a researcher in a hermetic dome whose only raw material is their own body, so the enclosure drives both fiction and mechanics ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 14:08](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=848)). Descent works the same way vertically:

> Through diving into the earth, the world is turned on its head. The rules that existed above no longer apply here. — [Everest Pipkin 2026, 28:52](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=1732)

Pipkin cites Undertale's fall into a world of monsters and Kentucky Route Zero's underground highway ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 28:52](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=1732)). In an unfinished prototype, Pipkin's angel digs caverns for a demanding god until they become a warren the player must learn and live in, and the question "is this about labour or love?" resolves into both, repetition and devotion ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 31:30](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=1890)). Alexandra Leonhart reads the fantasy dungeon as a Foucauldian *heterotopia*, a deviant space that juxtaposes objects and times, like a cemetery inside a city or a museum, and notes that Rogue's hero does not live there but comes from elsewhere to delve ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:11:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29463)).

### Theme carried by structure

A theme can live in how the rules behave rather than in what things are called. Joel Clark says Blaseball's pile-up of broken, layered rules is partly a deliberate experiment in replicating how broken real-world systems, especially American politics, come to exist: rules keep being added because gutting the system is nearly impossible, until the whole is incomprehensible ([Joel Clark 2020, 14:53](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=893)). Ada Null's Kiss Garden uses social-media-feed pacing, layering and rapid change, to create chaos and overwhelm while going nowhere, which reinforces its theme of stagnation instead of undercutting it ([Ada Null 2025, 8:39](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=519)).

### When the setting is the player's screen

G blekkenhorst's interface games push setting to its limit. *Metalepsis* is movement between levels of reality; games usually achieve "convergent metalepsis" by anchoring to a real location, but an interface game incorporates the player's hardware and body, so its geography is wherever it is played, much as found-footage films and epistolary novels make the reader a character by claiming to be evidence ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 6:49](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=409)). They work because real life is already mediated by screens we trust, so something magical or dangerous behind an interface feels as real as a message from your boss or grandmother ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 11:45](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=705)). Everyday frustration with technology becomes fiction: in The Archive, entering a player-made forgery crashes the database because the artefact is too powerful to be contained ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 14:53](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=893)). Most such games use a lean pretext of fictional employment, which is relatable and can valorise mundane screen work ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 15:26](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=926)).

**In practice**, ask of a candidate setting:

- What new mechanics does this theme suggest that a generic fantasy dungeon would not ([Josh Ge 2018, 20:15](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1215))?
- What shared "key" will make generated content feel like it belongs together ([Matt Carney 2026, 19:03](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1143))?
- How much familiarity does it give for free, and where will you need greebles to bridge the gap ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 16:22](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=982))?
- Where is the edge of the world, and what rules change inside it ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 13:27](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=807))?
- Could the structure of your rules, not just their names, carry the theme ([Joel Clark 2020, 14:53](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=893); [Ada Null 2025, 8:39](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=519))?
- Do you genuinely care about this lore, and does it generate play ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 20:39](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1239))?

## Writing the words: items, logs, dialogue and voice

Julian Day's starting point is that every presentation decision builds the world: graphics or ASCII, monster memory, item lookup. How you impart information goes further: if lore arrives in prose, your world has prose; if it arrives in poetry, your world has poetry ([Julian Day 2020, 4:14](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=254)). The words are part of the setting, and in a roguelike most of them appear in small, repeated places.

### Use the channels players already read

Jim Shepard's case against walls of text uses a late-game screen from Castle of the Winds, a game he loves: it is dense and rigid, the developer dictates how information arrives, the player can't make it their own, and three paragraphs make even engaged players want to skip ([Jim Shepard 2018, 3:56](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=236)). His alternative is the combat log. A wolf "deals four damage with sharp canines" and "howls mournfully and dies"; an unfamiliar monster attacks with "molten slashers" and defends with "deflected phasic chitin". The player learns about the creature because the information happens to them in a fight they must have anyway, and names like "dire" or "apex" sell fierceness ([Jim Shepard 2018, 8:25](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=505)).

Item text is the other high-traffic channel. Shepard calls item names, descriptions and flavour the easiest way to convey tone, because players look at loot constantly. Dungeonmans' starting weapon, a thick plank with a bent nail, is funny but still plausible, unlike a wet noodle you couldn't hurt anyone with, and it sets up a rags-to-riches arc as higher-tier items get more serious ([Jim Shepard 2016, 9:13](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=553)). Tangledeep goes further and characterises its heroine Mirai entirely through flavour text written as her thoughts about each item: she expects better swords, is baffled by strange magic, and the Wild Child job's claws prompt her to wonder whether she is a cold-blooded killer ([Jim Shepard 2018, 12:42](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=762)). The waste case is flavour text that restates the item ("a long sword is a weapon"): it costs reading time, writing time and, since translators charge per word, localisation money ([Jim Shepard 2018, 10:39](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=639)).

### Optional and brief

Lore that players can skip should be safe to skip. Paul Dean assumed Pacific Drive's players would not read lore, or would read it at random, so he kept it bite-sized and non-essential, a reward for the curious and never an obstacle for others ([Paul Dean 2025, 11:22](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=682)). Shepard likes optional books in the Elder Scrolls style, but warns that books meander from the core story and that mandatory plot information placed in them may never be read ([Jim Shepard 2018, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=306)). Day's long poem in a modernised Spenserian stanza in Shadow of the Wyrm is optional by design: it tells early-world lore for players who like lore ([Julian Day 2020, 6:08](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=368)).

On length, Dean and Francesco Cottone both argue for short. Dean's formative example is Captain Blood, where releasing a young alien on a planet without atmosphere produced two or three lines of him suffocating and missing his parents before he died; taken elsewhere, the alien was excited instead ([Paul Dean 2025, 4:53](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=293)). Dean still remembers it 35 years later:

> Good narrative doesn't have to be wordy, complex or elaborate. — [Paul Dean 2025, 4:53](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=293)

He points to Nuclear Throne's single-line interstitials, lines you could miss if you look away, that hint at the world and the character's feelings without compromising tone or pacing ([Paul Dean 2025, 6:06](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=366)). Francesco Cottone notes that Rogue itself tells the player what happened in short sentences, and that short sentences can carry complex stories while fitting the tight space of Chronicles of Stampadia's printed lookup tables ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 7:08](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=428)).

### Craft tools

The talks give a set of concrete techniques, most of them from Shepard's experience writing Tangledeep:

- **Pick a narrative perspective and keep it.** Item text can be third person (neutral description), second person (a narrator addressing the player like a dungeon master) or first person (the character's voice). Shepard admits mixing third and second by accident and recommends consistency. First person is the most powerful: the same ornate plate can reveal a complaining, pompous or loot-hungry character, while stats, sprite and slot carry the critical facts ([Jim Shepard 2018, 15:11](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=911)).
- **Borrow a voice.** As a rookie technique, take a fictional character you know well and apply their voice wholesale: a young blacksmith with Deckard Cain's love of history, patience and riddles. For Tangledeep's antagonist Shara he blended an idealistic early Jaina Proudmoore with Final Fantasy XII's Vayne Solidor ([Jim Shepard 2018, 19:43](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1183)).
- **Information first, flavour second.** A shop must read as a shop before the jokes; you don't serve a brick of salt with chicken sprinkled on top. Be concise unless the character is meant to ramble, and keep each voice consistent ([Jim Shepard 2018, 18:15](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1095)).
- **Work around what you can't write.** Shepard got stuck rhyming every scroll (nothing rhymes with "toxic"), so scroll text became the heroine's imperfect translations of runes, "dirt fold", "fat wet splash", which also made her more interesting ([Jim Shepard 2018, 13:44](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=824)).
- **Foreshadow with proper nouns.** Early items have little to say mechanically, so let one mention a named steel that great weapons are forged from; when the name reappears on plate mail or a golem, the player knows it is special ([Jim Shepard 2018, 11:23](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=683)).
- **Build twists from small facts.** A twist only matters if the player knows what is being twisted, so establish just the pertinent facts in small bites from characters and found objects, as BioShock does ([Jim Shepard 2018, 26:24](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1584)).
- **Audio logs, if you can afford them.** They deliver story without interrupting play, but voice acting is usually beyond indie roguelike budgets ([Jim Shepard 2018, 5:54](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=354)).
- **Keep a fallback for plot exposition.** Tarn Adams describes using traditional RPG devices at a dungeon such as a bandit hideout, incriminating notes, payments, or a captured villain confessing, so the game can pass information to the next link of a generated plot even when investigation is weak ([Tarn Adams 2018, 23:22](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1402)).
- **Generic systems, specific messages.** Alexei Pepers was inspired by how NetHack seems to know what you are doing whatever you have become, telling a floating eye it got cream pie in its eye, and that this comes from one readable body-part function rather than countless special cases. That combination makes the game feel like an all-knowing dungeon master ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 29:28](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1768)).

### Poetry and evocative prose

A handful of roguelikes take the opposite of the plain-and-short route and earn it by placing the richness carefully. Day credits ADOM's minstrel, whose poems deliver information about places, people and lore, as a new and still rare use of poetry in roguelikes; you don't need him for a regular win, but he is central in several ways ([Julian Day 2020, 3:05](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=185)). In Shadow of the Wyrm, Day wrote prose poems, paragraph poems rather than blocks of verse, into the descriptions shown by the item lookup command, and players told him how nice it was to stumble on them inside an otherwise violent game ([Julian Day 2020, 10:15](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=615)). For his stanzas he uses modern diction and imperfect rhymes such as "dread" and "stretch" to widen the rhyme set ([Julian Day 2020, 8:09](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=489)), and he breaks lines mid-sentence, leaves the middle lines unrhymed and closes with an alexandrine for a more natural rhythm than his Spenserian model ([Julian Day 2020, 8:22](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=502)).

Younès Rabii finds the same habit in La Horde du Contrevent and Caves of Qud: poetic description of trivial things, such as a pile of bones that makes you think about time and life, evokes the world's beauty, danger and wonder ([Younès Rabii 2022, 12:27](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=747)). Ivy Melinda calls Qud's prose the purplest she has seen and argues that it, together with a lovingly depicted, diverse cast in safe hub locations, makes the world feel real and alive beyond its mechanics ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 4:34](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=274)). Ray notes that Qud attaches handwritten "recall stories" to storied artefacts with no attributed teller, so they read like a storyteller digressing about provenance ([Ray 2025, 7:01](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=421)).

**In practice**, for a first pass over your game's words:

- Decide the delivery form on purpose, prose, poetry, log lines, first-person thoughts, because the form is part of the world ([Julian Day 2020, 4:14](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=254)).
- Move story out of text screens and into the combat log, monster names and item text ([Jim Shepard 2018, 3:56](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=236); [Jim Shepard 2018, 8:25](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=505)).
- Delete any flavour text that only restates the item ([Jim Shepard 2018, 10:39](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=639)).
- Choose one perspective and one voice per character, and put the necessary information first ([Jim Shepard 2018, 15:11](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=911); [Jim Shepard 2018, 18:15](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1095)).
- Keep optional lore short and never put required information only there ([Paul Dean 2025, 11:22](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=682); [Jim Shepard 2018, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=306)).
- Where you want richness, tuck it where curious players will find it, in lookup text or a minstrel's verse, rather than in their path ([Julian Day 2020, 10:15](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=615); [Julian Day 2020, 3:05](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=185)).

## Authored story inside a replayable structure

The previous section dealt with words one line at a time. The remaining sections deal with structure: how authored story is arranged so that it survives replay, and how generated characters, histories and plots are made to read as stories.

A roguelike is played many times, in many orders, by a player who keeps dying. Any handwritten story you put inside it has to survive that. The obvious move, a story that branches on what the player does, is the one two talks warn scales worst ([Nic Junius 2024, 8:01](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=481); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 3:48](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=228)).

### Why branching breaks down

Nic Junius, whose theatre analogy appears under "Players as co-authors", puts the problem bluntly: a narrative that reacts to player actions breeds fractally branching trees of alternate realities, and the authoring burden quickly becomes untenable. Tools help, but it is hard to know when systemic authoring actually becomes cheaper than writing by hand, and combinatorial systems often call for more content than anyone can reasonably write ([Nic Junius 2024, 8:01](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=481)). His starting principle is that however dynamic the system, someone still has to put pen to paper for every piece, so you choose a story structure with authoring cost in mind ([Nic Junius 2024, 7:18](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=438)).

Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster agree that handwritten branching narrative is the gold standard for emotional impact, and that it scales poorly: mapping cascading consequences over dozens of choices is bounded by labour and budget. Their example is Hades, which feels handwritten and responsive because it is, built on an enormous list of conditions and over 20,000 unique voice lines. Hades generates its levels but not its story ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 3:48](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=228)). Nathan Savant makes the same observation from the other side: Hades gets its reactivity almost entirely through dialogue, with relatively simple triggers but huge scripts of conditional lines, rather than by moving characters around the world ([Nathan Savant 2026, 14:24](https://youtu.be/rmddpcmIJ2I?t=864)). The lesson in both readings is that Hades' reactivity comes from simple triggers over a very large volume of handwritten lines, which is what makes it so costly.

### Braided narrative

Junius' answer is the *braided narrative*: a structure of individual linear storylines whose progression is controlled by both independent and shared state conditions ([Nic Junius 2024, 11:15](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=675)). Each strand is linear, so writing it grows roughly linearly. The variety comes from *when* a player meets each piece, not from branching on everything the player does. Ideally the strands share a cast and complementary themes, so they read as one story twisted together rather than parallel ones ([Nic Junius 2024, 11:15](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=675)).

The two kinds of condition do different jobs. Independent conditions keep the strands distinct. Shared conditions make them move together, sharing momentum and timeliness, and they invite players to connect strands whether or not you spell the connection out. If every strand advanced only on its own conditions, you would drift back toward the combinatorial tree ([Nic Junius 2024, 14:21](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=861)). Junius reserves shared states mostly for major beats of the central plot. A side story that reaches such a beat simply pauses until the player gets there, so you never write content for a player arriving out of order, side stories can refer to plot events without extra branches, and a player who exhausts the side content is pushed to advance the main plot ([Nic Junius 2024, 16:42](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1002)).

Hades is his main case study:

- **The spine runs through runs.** The credits roll after the player reaches the surface and beats their father ten times. Because the game is hard, players rarely see much of the central story in their first ten runs, so the side stories carry the pacing and give non-mechanical reasons to keep playing past the credits ([Nic Junius 2024, 20:19](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1219)).
- **Varied gates.** Character storylines are gated on a relationship meter filled by gifts, on how many times you have spoken to someone, on run-count breakpoints, and even on the difficulty-customisation system, all independent of main-story progress. One player finishes the main story with little side progress; another finishes most side stories before the credits ([Nic Junius 2024, 22:41](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1361)).
- **A subset of the cast per run.** Only some characters are reachable on a given escape attempt, and even then you may lack the resources to progress them. Junius calls this the trick of the whole braid: players cannot advance any strand at will, and keep discovering more after dozens of hours ([Nic Junius 2024, 23:34](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1414)).
- **A pacing cap.** Pure if-statements are not enough, because without a cap the player gets every available story unit at once and must pace it themselves. Hades tends to release at most about three new story events per run. Tying progression to other systems also rewards engaging with them ([Nic Junius 2024, 18:21](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1101)).

Fire Emblem: Three Houses shows the same idea on a relationship graph. Its large cast would explode combinatorially, so support conversations are mutual (each pair has one linear set of scenes, with no direction to the relationship) and are unlocked almost entirely by the two characters fighting side by side. Only a few final conversations are gated on main-plot beats ([Nic Junius 2024, 27:03](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1623)).

Junius is candid about the limit. Both games contain an obscene amount of writing, and the burden still grows with scope. What changes is the curve: a braid scales like writing linear stories, not like a branching tree or exhaustive coverage of a dynamic system ([Nic Junius 2024, 29:32](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1772)).

### Storylets and salience

A *storylet* is a self-contained chunk of authored content with a condition on it; *salience* is how the engine decides which eligible storylet fits best right now ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:33:08](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23588)). Several independent projects converge on storylets as the practical unit for story in a replayable game.

- **Voyageur.** Bruno Dias built his space game on Fallen London-style storylets gated by planet and player traits. Outcomes change traits, which act as stats, meters and spendable resources: spacing a stowaway raises ruthlessness and lowers kindness, taking them in does the reverse, and that shifts crew loyalty and later options ([Bruno Dias 2016, 15:17](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=917)).
- **Hintline 93.** Paris Buttfield-Addison describes a museum exhibit about 1993 game support lines in which each call plays like a roguelike run, drawn from a shuffle bag of about 52 calls. In Yarn Spinner every call node shares a title, forming a node group; since every condition passes, the engine picks a random, least-recently-seen call, so visitors queueing behind each other rarely hear the same one. One call per file let five people write at once ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:33:08](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23588)).
- **Sunshine Shuffle.** Stav Hinenzon's poker game treats each conversation as a storylet with preconditions and post-conditions. The story is a linear sequence of main conversations plus optional ones unlocked along the way; whenever the table needs talk, one is picked by weighted randomness from the next main conversation and any unlocked optional ones ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=226)). Poker and story run simultaneously and independently, so characters bet, speak and pass in one flowing scene ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 1:30](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=90)), and keeping dialogue, cards and menus in the same boat cabin makes the characters seem alive, like actors doing secondary business while delivering lines ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 13:05](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=785)).

The same idea works on paper. Francesco Cottone describes how Fallout: The Board Game delivers non-linear story with encounter cards: a decision on one card may tell you to shuffle a numbered card into a deck, so the consequence surfaces later somewhere else, and several storylines can interleave in one adventure ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 6:23](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=383)). In a digital game, Alexander Birke's Sea of Rifts writes choice-based scenes in the open-source Ink language and adds an in-house editor alongside each Ink file that connects choices to game state, so a choice can change the state, be disabled when you lack the right crew, or be resolved randomly or by skill check ([Alexander Birke 2024, 19:44](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1184)). That bridge between authored text and simulation state is what turns a story chunk into a storylet.

### Giving fragments a shape

Storylets alone give you a shuffle. Three techniques give the shuffle a shape. Paul Dean recommends gating: a universal introduction that teaches mechanics and key characters, then wide freedom in the middle. With fixed points at each end there are a hundred ways between them, and how much hand-holding you add is a choice about how punishing or helpful you want to be ([Paul Dean 2025, 25:13](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1513)). Bruno Dias borrows perpetual forward motion from 80 Days: the player can never revisit a place, so they pick up threads, play with them briefly and move on, and no single generated planet has to carry much narrative weight ([Bruno Dias 2016, 14:10](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=850)). And Herbert Wolverson shows how a level generator can order beats spatially. If you know the room order along the *hot path* (the route the player must take), you can place story beats such as a destiny speech near room one, and place a lock-and-key puzzle validly: a flood fill confirms there is no way past room five, so the key must spawn in rooms one to four ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:11](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1451)).

### Fixed text, varied encounter

You can also keep every word authored and vary only the order or the view. Chelsea Thompto's A Walk in the Dark fixes six authored six-line poems; when one ends, the next is chosen at random and the spaces they appear in are shuffled and reordered ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 9:33](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=573)). The Neutrinowatch podcast pushes this further. In one episode music swells over a monologue in waves that shift daily, so each listen reveals only parts of the story and the whole emerges only across several days ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 20:38](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=1238)). In another, an AI character keeps rewriting a letter, and its text drifts from plain to abstract and weird over the month ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 14:28](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=868)).

Varying the *size* of authored pieces is another lever. Alexei Pepers points to Yakuza 0's substories: most use two verbs, but one unexpectedly contains a unique zombie-defence mode with nothing signalling it in advance. That unevenness creates content suspense, because the player never knows how big or strange the next piece will be, and Pepers notes small games can do it too ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 47:30](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2850)). Hidden alternatives work similarly. Isaac Io Schankler's Orb Pondering Simulator hides two endings behind the same small verb set, so which one a crowd reaches depends on which command it tries first ([Isaac Io Schankler 2024, 15:19](https://youtu.be/M6t5W5PPVW0?t=919)).

### When the script meets the simulation

If authored scenes use systemic objects, the script must bend to the simulation. Rich Wilson describes a Dishonored poisoning scene where the wine bottle and glasses were real, breakable objects. He scripted listeners for breakage and a branch in which, if the glasses are broken, the poisoner lures the victim to the basement and stabs him instead; having done the work, he added "spill the glasses" to the context menu so more players would find it ([Rich Wilson 2021, 9:26](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=566)). Budget for this: every systemic prop in a scripted scene is a branch you may have to write.

Aaron A. Reed offers a different way out of the immersion assumption altogether, a fourth position beside the frame, resonance and cooperation views discussed under "Let the player's imagination do the work". Procedural stories do not have to be immersive. In Ice-Bound players manipulate symbols and watch the consequences ripple through the whole story, and Reed argues that a god's-eye view of the narrative machine can make multilinear structure more meaningful than immersion would ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 20:45](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1245)).

> Procedural stories don't have to be immersive. — [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 20:45](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1245)

### Choosing a structure

The talks do not give a formula, but they line up into a rough guide:

- **Small team, short runs, lots of replays:** a shuffle bag or storylet pool with simple conditions and least-recently-seen selection, as in Hintline 93, where one-file-per-storylet also lets several writers work in parallel ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:33:08](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23588)). Add forward motion so no single piece has to carry much weight ([Bruno Dias 2016, 14:10](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=850)).
- **A story that should develop across many runs:** a braid of linear strands with independent gates, a few shared gates on main beats, a subset of characters per run and a cap on new events per run ([Nic Junius 2024, 16:42](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1002); [Nic Junius 2024, 18:21](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1101); [Nic Junius 2024, 23:34](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1414)). Expect the writing load to grow with scope, roughly linearly ([Nic Junius 2024, 29:32](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1772)).
- **Story that must react to game state:** storylets whose conditions and outcomes read and write that state, as in Voyageur and Sea of Rifts ([Bruno Dias 2016, 15:17](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=917); [Alexander Birke 2024, 19:44](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1184)), with scripted scenes listening for what the simulation can do to their props ([Rich Wilson 2021, 9:26](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=566)).
- **Avoid** full branching unless you have Hades-scale writing resources ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 3:48](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=228)).

## Procedural characters and a world that notices

A generated character starts as a bundle of numbers and tags. The work of this section is turning that bundle into someone the player remembers. The talks converge on two moves: let generation lead into handwritten material, and make the game visibly notice what has happened to each character ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 3:11](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=191); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 18:50](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1130); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:58](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=358)).

### Wildermyth: generation that leads into handwriting

Wildermyth is the case several speakers reach for independently. Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner state its core goal as character and story moments that feel unique to each playthrough yet genuine and memorable, achieved by having random generation guide or lead into handcrafted content across three pillars: heroes, myths (events) and combat ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 3:11](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=191)). Jamie Brittain describes the result as heavily authored stories whose people are procedurally generated, ageing, mutating, retiring and returning, so the game gets intimate moments and a sense of time passing against an epic backdrop ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 21:36](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1296)). McHorse and Foster note that Wildermyth interleaves requirement-based procedural events with handwritten arcs whose villains have real motivation, falling back to more generic procedural arcs when the custom ones run out. That mix widens the stories a budget can tell, but it still bounds them: players always want to do or romance something you did not plan for ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:58](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=358)).

The developers' practical rules are the most transferable part:

- **Acknowledge what happened by chance, not only what was chosen.** One-line "tidings" between battles reference transformations and their follow-ups, such as a hero carving art with a hook hand. The player did not choose the lost hand, so they discover the hero's story while guiding it, and Belanger and Wagner find that just as impactful as reacting to choices ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 18:50](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1130)).
- **Add variation wherever its absence would feel weird.** An estranged father should comment on his child's new animal head, even in a single panel; one acknowledging panel is enough to satisfy players ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 17:00](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1020)).
- **Let traits change the scene, not just the text.** Panel splits, where a hero's trait changes how a scene plays out (a wolf hero sniffing out a cave, a fire-touched hero trivialising a skill check in an ice cave), convince players events are not templates. Ask which trait you would expect to dramatically alter this encounter ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 15:23](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=923)).
- **Write every voice.** Wildermyth writes text splits for all eleven personalities; letting a few personalities share lines proved inadequate, because consistent voices are essential to a game about memorable heroes ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 13:21](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=801)).
- **No caricatures.** When any hero can fill any role, personalities cannot be extreme and relationships must stay broadly friendly. A hero who only speaks in poetry, or two heroes who hate each other, cannot be kept consistent across every event, so even rivals in Wildermyth still work together ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 14:03](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=843)).
- **Exclude rather than vary when that is cheaper.** A fall-into-a-hole event simply does not trigger for winged heroes ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 17:20](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1040)).

Brittain draws a broader claim from games like this: a procedurally generated cast inside a hero story breaks down the hierarchies that narrative structures tend to reinforce, much as a diverse writers' room keeps stories from "rounding themselves down", and with permadeath giving events consequence it makes roguelikes engines for character development ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 22:55](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1375)). Aaron A. Reed reports something compatible from Blue Lacuna: players sensed and valued a dynamic relationship with a character far more than the simulation of objects, so he chose to put his effort into immersing people in a character rather than an environment ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 7:00](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=420)).

### Character arcs from hidden state

Max Kreminski's work on Star Freighter gives a generator-level account of how arcs can emerge. His first point is about pacing: relationships take time, and generators tend to dump a full trait list up front. He acknowledges Tanya Short's argument that visible traits help players notice characters have inner lives at all, but prefers revealing traits gradually through actions over many interactions, as real life and other stories do ([Max Kreminski 2017, 6:15](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=375)).

Hidden state then makes foreshadowing possible. Foreshadowing normally needs knowledge of the future, but if a character has a *latent* trait (a dark secret, an untapped potential), storylets can drop hints about it before it develops. In Star Freighter a storylet fires only for a character with latent fighting potential: after a near-fatal fight they decide to learn self-defence, and a later storylet brings aboard a martial-arts passenger to teach them ([Max Kreminski 2017, 8:21](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=501)). Hintline 93 uses the same principle in miniature: it picks the next event first, then shows flavour text leaning toward it, so the phone "already knows things" before the know-it-all caller rings. Buttfield-Addison says roguelikes do this as well ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:28:25](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23305)).

Kreminski adds three further ideas; he flags the first and third as speculative or not yet implemented, while the second is a Star Freighter example:

- **Best and worst endings.** Adapting Emily Short's advice, generate a good and a bad outcome for every significant character in advance and offer storylets that let the player bring either about, for instance by making characters' goals incompatible ([Max Kreminski 2017, 15:05](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=905)).
- **Storylet chains.** A fugitive passenger acts nervous about a heavily policed destination (foreshadowing from a hidden trait); the game raises the chance of a random search because contraband is aboard, since searches that find nothing are dull; the player then chooses to hide the fugitive or turn them in, a manual version of offering that character's best or worst outcome ([Max Kreminski 2017, 17:32](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1052)).
- **Focus episodes.** Like a TV episode centred on one character, a drama manager tracks which characters are in focus and up-weights storylets involving them, revealing backstory and deepening the connection, which also makes a later death sadder ([Max Kreminski 2017, 14:40](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=880)).

Kreminski also names a choice every such system faces. You can retroactively give a character a secret because the plot needs drama now, which he accepts as valid in other contexts, or you can set state first and let events fall out of it. He prefers the simulationist route and calls backfilling "cheating" for his own system ([Max Kreminski 2017, 20:46](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1246)).

### Speech that comes from somewhere

Generated characters sound authored when what they say is anchored to something. Mark R Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum ends culture generation by building a database of culture-specific reference points for each domain (war, family, love, death, religion) that NPCs draw on in speech. NPCs from one culture might all fixate on the same ancient battle they won, which teaches the player the world and makes it feel lived in ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 14:36](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=876)).

Robin Sloan makes the same argument about generated text in general: pin it to a systematic framework such as a map, a dramatis personae, a family tree, a spell list or a bestiary. The framework acts as a rhythm section that keeps the beat while the language riffs, and text, which already offloads work to the reader's imagination, does so more strongly when anchored ([Robin Sloan 2019, 19:24](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1164)). In his own project he fed the generated place names from each reader's map into the text generator, so the story could say "on the road towards Ningbag" and the reader could trace the route; he calls the names the glue between map and story ([Robin Sloan 2019, 7:27](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=447)). For conversations that need memory, Kate Compton keeps the logic in plain JavaScript and rewrites Tracery grammar rules at runtime, pushing a value onto a symbol when characters start discussing something and pulling it off later, treating the grammar as a whiteboard ([Kate Compton 2016, 29:35](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1775)).

**In practice:**

- Let generation choose *who*, and handwriting decide *what it means* ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 3:11](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=191)).
- Reference random misfortunes, and add a line wherever silence would feel odd ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 18:50](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1130); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 17:00](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1020)).
- Keep personalities within a range every event can support ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 14:03](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=843)).
- Hold some traits hidden and hint at them before they surface ([Max Kreminski 2017, 8:21](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=501)).
- Anchor speech to generated culture, places and names ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 14:36](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=876); [Robin Sloan 2019, 7:27](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=447)).

## Generated history and environmental storytelling

Several roguelikes generate a past for their world. The convergent technique is not to show that past as a chronicle but to scatter it into the world as objects the player stumbles on ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 49:44](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2984); [Isaac Karth 2019, 12:44](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=764)). The harder question, which the talks raise more than they answer, is why a player would care ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 7:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=429)).

### History as artefacts

Caves of Qud is the canonical example. It generates the life histories of ancient sultans each game, inscribes them in a historical record, and then surfaces scenes from that record on shrines, artefacts and snippets throughout the world; a shrine might depict a battle or a tavern visit ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 49:44](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2984)). Players meet that history at real in-game locations through shrines, engravings and paintings, such as one about a sultan adopted as a baby by gamblers ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 34:39](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=2079)). Village histories get the same treatment: slime-filled amphoras that have a cooking use are also painted with scenes from the village's past, so ordinary props become monuments to events in the village's history ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 15:36](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=936)).

Dwarf Fortress does this with engravings and artefact descriptions. Isaac Karth notes that although the player never sees the world-generation history simulation directly, they experience its effects indirectly through that surface content ([Isaac Karth 2019, 12:44](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=764)). Ivy Melinda describes what makes this work in Qud: the sultan histories are assembled like jigsaw pieces pulled blindly from a bag and crammed together in the hope of coherence, and that roughness leaves room for players to interpret and build their own stories, as Dwarf Fortress's histories do. One statue recounts a sultan saved by a band of worms after driving a carriage off the road, and forever indebted to them ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 2:35](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=155)).

### Forgetting on purpose

Cole Wehrle's board game Oath, whose post-game reports and journal appear under "Players as co-authors", argues for something most generators do not do: forget. Oath has a deliberately selective memory, fully remembering some things, partially remembering others and not recording the rest; Wehrle pairs this with a decision framework that sharpens regret, and calls a faulty memory plus regret the essence of good history-telling ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 14:38](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=878)). He goes further: the gaps in the record are what make it feel real, and forgetting is probably the most central part of history ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 29:33](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1773)).

> The gaps in the record are the thing that makes the record feel so real. — [Cole Wehrle 2025, 29:33](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1773)

This sits against the full-record approaches later in this section, where every event is kept and browsable. The two are not exclusive. Qud and Dwarf Fortress keep a full record internally but surface only fragments, which produces gaps at the level the player sees ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 49:44](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2984); [Isaac Karth 2019, 12:44](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=764)). Wehrle's position is stronger: the record itself should be incomplete.

### Ruins and interpretation

Florence Smith Nicholls treats environmental storytelling as archaeology, because it means interpreting the material remains of an imagined past ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2025, 6:44](https://youtu.be/9kqvF2TqxLo?t=404)). Her example is Mike Cook's Nothing Beside Remains, an ASCII-style game with a generated ruined desert village and no win state; its implicit goal is to work out what happened ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2025, 6:44](https://youtu.be/9kqvF2TqxLo?t=404)). The objects present and their replacement-grammar descriptions depend on which of three causes ended the village: wildlife, environmental factors, or overpopulation leading to starvation ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 4:11](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=251)). That is a compact design: one hidden cause, many objects whose presence and wording follow from it, and a player left to infer.

She proposes making the descriptions themselves subjective by giving the protagonist one of several roles, such as archaeologist, tourist or poet, each seeing objects differently. She was wary that the archaeologist would read as the "good" or authoritative view, so the roles overlap and none is privileged; the aim is partly to satirise the lone-traveller-discovers-ruins trope rooted in colonial ideas of archaeology ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 6:07](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=367)). She points to Disco Elysium, where objects speak to you with their own opinions, and Heaven's Vault, where earlier translations shape how you read new artefact fragments, as models for objects with a point of view and for interpretation that accumulates ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2022, 7:52](https://youtu.be/IanNZxUaVQs?t=472)). Younès Rabii finds the same role-gating in the novel La Horde du Contrevent and in Dwarf Fortress: each character understands the world deeply in one domain only, so which stories you can access depends on characters' jobs and skills ([Younès Rabii 2022, 13:43](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=823)).

### Why would anyone care?

Making history available is not the same as making it matter. Jonathan Lessard states the problem directly: accessible simulation history does not explain why players would care about thousands of fictional people and their minor details. He does not claim to have solved it, but his team found that playing a single character made it unlikely that one life would be interesting, whereas a game role that gave reasons to look at many characters made interesting stories more likely to surface ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 7:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=429)). His interface supplies leads: per-character pages with family tabs, hyperlinked year-by-year timelines and graphs of values such as influence. A woman with a husband and two ex-husbands, children with different surnames, or a sudden drop in influence in some year each raise a question to dig into ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 5:22](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=322)). Intervention adds a personal stake. Lessard used a miracle to move Jessica near Valerie, whom she was courting with poetry; she joined a clan there, died in a battle, and almost no one came to her funeral. That consequence is visible only by examining the chronicles, which gives the player a reason to look ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 11:21](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=681)). Bad News does something similar after its play session ends, simulating the town forward thirty years to produce an epilogue of what became of the characters the player met ([Bad News team 2016, 1:09:13](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=4153)).

Dustin Freeman is more critical of world-history generation as it usually ships. In Dwarf Fortress, Minecraft or SimEarth, it is passive scenery, like an opening cutscene; players engage with it only by stopping out of curiosity to pull on a thread such as an item's lore ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 12:38](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=758)). His Spirit of the Ages makes history-making the play: the player uplifts a crocodile into dwarves, or sand into anxious sand golems, by choosing likes, dislikes and a destiny, and these become persistent concerns that carry on outside their original context so he does not have to anticipate everything ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 16:05](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=965)). Jasmine Otto reached a related conclusion from a family-tree module with long-lived vampires: a hands-off multi-generational simulation produces interesting artefacts to tab through afterwards, but it is not fun to sit and watch ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 7:42](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=462)).

Aaron A. Reed adds the cost side. Procedural story projects should simulate only what the story needs, because players rarely notice environmental detail that does not serve it ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 2:15](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=135)). Blue Lacuna had room descriptions that varied by time of day, a moon whose phases drove the tides, and weather-triggered ambient messages; players did not realise or care that a description had 18 variants, and what they noticed was not what they remembered ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 4:15](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=255)).

### Scoping history to what players meet

Taken together, the talks suggest working backwards from the player's encounter:

- Decide where history will surface (shrines, props, engravings, character pages) before deciding how much to simulate ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 15:36](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=936); [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 2:15](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=135)).
- Surface fragments, and consider genuinely forgetting some of the record ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 2:35](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=155); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 29:33](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1773)).
- Give the player a role or a lead that makes the past worth investigating ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 7:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=429); [Jonathan Lessard 2023, 5:22](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=322)).
- Where you can, let the player's actions become part of the history, so it is played rather than watched ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 16:05](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=965); [Jonathan Lessard 2023, 11:21](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=681)).

## Finding and staging the drama

A simulation that produces events has not yet produced a story. This is one of the clearest convergences in the chapter: researchers, live performers, a fan-data group and game developers all say that the step from output to story is a separate job, and someone has to do it ([Max Kreminski 2019, 13:29](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=809); [Bad News team 2016, 7:22](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=442); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:28](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=208); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:37](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=337)).

### Output is not story

Max Kreminski summarises James Ryan's model from his dissertation *Curating Simulated Storyworlds*. A simulation runs freely; its events are *chronicled*; the chronicle is *story-sifted* for the most narratively useful material; and a *narrativizer*, either a player's head or an AI, turns that material into a story. Nothing that comes straight out of the simulation is the emergent narrative ([Max Kreminski 2019, 13:29](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=809)). McHorse and Foster make the same point from experience: Dwarf Fortress generates interesting events, but a friend who tried to turn them into narrative, even after sifting for good bits such as a spy who had the tables turned on him, found them hard to convey. Connected information rendered fluently is still not a compelling narrative ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:37](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=337)).

Kreminski also names who suffers when the step is skipped. In dense roguelike simulations so much is happening in the interface and background that the compelling bits are buried, and that kind of storytelling is effectively closed to novices ([Max Kreminski 2020, 0:30](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=30)). Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi, speaking about the Blaseball fan data group SIBR, add the precondition: procedural systems constantly tell surprising stories that are impenetrable without detailed records, so emergent narrative depends on logging, as in a roguelike where you review the log to learn why something happened ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:01](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=181)). Once data is cheap, the storytelling problem becomes filtering signal from noise ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:28](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=208)).

### Sifting as a technique

*Story sifting* means letting the simulation produce an overwhelming chronicle, then searching it for compelling sequences to surface as micro-stories. Kreminski's example: character A starts a project and gives up, B comes along and talks about it, and A resumes work. The ideal is a large library of diverse sifting patterns, so many different micro-stories can be pulled from the same events ([Max Kreminski 2020, 1:34](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=94)). His group is using sifters to drive an artificial commentator that narrates the simulation as it runs ([Max Kreminski 2020, 8:40](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=520)).

Bad News, a live performance piece, shows the human version. A hidden "wizard" live-codes queries into a simulated town to find love triangles, rival businesses and founding families, and passes the material to an actor, who starts with about three to five dramatic high points to build into an arc ([Bad News team 2016, 2:30](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=150)). The narrator's framing is that this material is latent: it is not coded as story, but a human recognises it as interesting, and it only needs bringing to the surface. In the run shown, the chosen storyline was that the deceased had been in love with his brother's wife, and both worked at the family brewery ([Bad News team 2016, 7:22](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=442)). Bad News also allows what its team calls arbitrary simulation fidelity: when the simulation cannot handle what the player does, the wizard types in what is happening, as when a night janitor was made to emerge to let a locked-out player into a building ([Bad News team 2016, 39:55](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=2395)). A digital game cannot have a wizard, but it can have the equivalent: queries for dramatic patterns, and authored fallbacks where the simulation runs out.

Statistics are a cheap form of sifting. The SIBR speakers argue that aggregates, averages and leaderboards tell stories at a glance: a graph of a player's stats over time can show an underdog arc, and knowing averages lets a fan spot which opposing slugger to fear, or a lone star on a struggling team, without watching a game ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 11:21](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=681)).

### What to sift for: lessons from reality TV

Reality television is a genre built on sifting a constructed situation for drama, and three speakers use it as a model.

Dennis Greger gives a content hierarchy. At the top are rare moments of raw, unfiltered, relatable emotion; two of those make a strong episode. Below them come broken taboos (mostly social norms, such as lying to someone's face or who pays the bill), then characterisation, then "juice" (fast edits, music, colour, noise), and only then traditional story, which matters little because the show's format carries it ([Dennis Greger 2025, 2:35](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=155)). He notes that genuine emotion is why audiences return, and that the conversation about centring emotion is barely happening in games ([Dennis Greger 2025, 15:07](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=907)). For a story sifter, that is a ranking of what to look for.

> You really want to find raw emotion. You want to have these moments that are really few and far between. — [Dennis Greger 2025, 2:35](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=155)

Greger also explains the conditions that produce such moments. A *magic circle*, a bubble where normal rules do not apply, is why unusual things happen on a set; creators sustain it by holding tone, building trust and treating the game as seriously as the people inside it ([Dennis Greger 2025, 7:36](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=456)). And the narrative works like a party of rooms with heightened moods: you need not explain everything, and should not try, but you must make clear who we are looking at and give a clue to what they are doing ([Dennis Greger 2025, 10:35](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=635)). That last rule transfers directly to surfacing sifted events: name the actor, hint at the situation, and trust the player with the rest.

Leigh Alexander calls these shows *constructed realities*: contained spaces with rules designed to make social narrative emerge, which makes the celebrity mansion a natural roguelike dungeon ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 16:51](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1011)). Prototyping her game McMansion, her team found simulated celebrity behaviour so unhinged that they shifted from having the player solve murders toward having the player commit them ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 6:46](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=406)). Florence Smith Nicholls, reading Love Island as a roguelike, notes that the confessional, where the viewer learns what other characters do not know, is hard to translate to digital games but might suit live or hybrid design like Bad News ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 9:50](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=590)). She also finds in reality TV an "honesty of fakeness": contestants accused of playing the game are all, in fact, playing a game, which exposes how constructed our ideas about relationships are, and she offers this as a lens on how roguelikes approach simulation ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 11:53](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=713)).

**In practice:**

- Log everything the simulation does, in a form you can query ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:01](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=181)).
- Write sifting patterns for the micro-stories you want, and build many of them ([Max Kreminski 2020, 1:34](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=94)).
- Rank what you surface: raw emotion and broken social norms above plot ([Dennis Greger 2025, 2:35](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=155)).
- When you present a moment, say who it is about and give a clue to what is going on, and stop there ([Dennis Greger 2025, 10:35](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=635)).
- Use aggregate statistics and leaderboards as at-a-glance story ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 11:21](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=681)).
- Do not assume fluent text makes the material compelling ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:37](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=337)).

## Generating plot: planners, quests and complications

The previous sections find stories in what happened. This one is about making things happen so that a story results. The talks offer three broad families: simulation of agents, planning, and grammars borrowed from tabletop play and older media.

### The real problem is rewriting

Stephen G. Ware frames the field. Getting a computer to write a story is an old problem, dating back to Tale-Spin in 1974, and not the one games need; plenty of people want to write stories. The interesting problem is getting a computer to *rewrite* a story on the fly when a player does things the author cannot control, as a D&D game master does ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 1:14](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=74)). His main lesson is that storytelling is non-Markovian: whether an event makes sense depends on the whole sequence of past and future events and on the alternatives, so a story's quality can only be judged relative to the other stories that could have been told. That is why planning stories is expensive: all the alternatives have to be generated and checked ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 20:11](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1211)).

### Emergence versus planning

Ware sets out the basic trade-off. Emergent stories from many lightweight agents, as in Dwarf Fortress or The Sims, are unpredictable, so if you have beats you must hit, you can only hope they happen; you are herding virtual cats. Planned stories look ahead to guarantee requirements can be met. Handwritten scripts sit at the other end, limited to what can be imagined in advance ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 3:07](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=187)).

Jasmine Otto's experience shows the emergent failure in practice. She built a faction simulation with murders and accusations, wanting an event where someone is dramatically accused of murder to fire. With so many characters retaliating tit-for-tat, steering toward that event was painful; the system was interesting but did not give her leverage, which is what motivated her cyclic plot generation ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 9:31](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=571)). Max Kreminski names what is missing: generated stories need character-level goals ("perform my experiment", "get revenge on Fred") to make scenes compelling, and author-level goals ("raise the tension between these characters", "illustrate a conflict between two values") to keep the story moving instead of becoming a soup of characters acting aimlessly ([Max Kreminski 2019, 21:35](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1295)).

Ware describes how story planners supply that structure:

- **Intention.** A classical planner happily produces nonsense, such as a merchant walking to your house and giving you medicine.
