The first story planners required every action to contribute to some character's goal, propagating intentions backward, so the player walking to market and buying medicine for their grandmother is explained by the goal, and so is the merchant's reason for selling ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 8:34](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=514)).
- **Failure.** Stories run on conflict, so plans must be able to fail. A planner can explain an action in a failed plan, like walking to a crossroads and being robbed, by drawing on the many unused stories its search generated: an action makes sense if there exists some story in which it does. The discarded stories become a database of what could have happened ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 10:41](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=641)).
- **Intervention or replanning.** When the player is about to make the planned story impossible, a drama manager can intervene and stop the action, or, ideally, accommodate it by replanning around it. Fast planning is what makes replanning possible ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 15:39](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=939)).

### Tabletop methods: surprise, coherence and failing forward

Cezar Capacle brings techniques from solo and GM-less tabletop play. The sweet spot for a generated result balances surprise against confirmed expectations, so that a revelation feels as if it had been foreshadowed; when it works, players say "of course that's the answer" and feel clever for connecting earlier random events, and the story can surprise more than anything written in advance ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 10:09](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=609)). His second tool is *fail forward*: a failed test should create complications and new avenues rather than a dead end. A failed lock-pick roll under old binary resolution just stalled the story, and without a GM you need tools that push it onward ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 13:22](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=802)). He is also clear about the cost. With about a third of results landing in partial success, players must constantly invent complications in long sessions, which either turns repetitive ("you get hurt") or piles up threats until the original mission is unrecognisable ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 18:13](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1093)). If you generate complications automatically, you need variety in them and a limit on how many accumulate.

### Quest grammars

Nathan Savant offers a grammar for programmer-developers who are not writers. Quests are stories, so they decompose into a beginning, a middle and an end, each with its own component types that a system can combine ([Nathan Savant 2021, 1:44](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=104)). He builds the parts from The Lord of the Rings:

- **Acceptance.** A quest can be accepted, rejected, rejected and later accepted, or rejected and forced on the protagonist anyway. Frodo accepts; a player might walk away, come back out of guilt, or be dragged back by Gandalf. Each response changes how the rest of the quest reads without extra writing ([Nathan Savant 2021, 3:51](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=231)).
- **Triggers.** A quest can start by conscious choice, by implied choice (entering a spider's nest, making noise), or with no choice at all, like the One Ring's quest ([Nathan Savant 2021, 5:40](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=340)). The concrete mechanisms are talking to a character, interacting with an object such as a job board or treasure map, gaining an item, gaining knowledge, entering an area, or using a verb, such as casting an outlawed spell that puts you on the run ([Nathan Savant 2021, 6:43](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=403)).
- **Middle struggles.** Scripted events, changed or new environments, and mechanical stresses like status effects that change how the player must play. Wearing the Ring flags Frodo for the ringwraiths, so he cannot follow roads or light fires ([Nathan Savant 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=486)).
- **The end.** Usually a return to normal. Because gameplay and interface alterations are exhausting, reserve the significant ones for the main quest and pace them; in the books only the main quest heavily alters "gameplay" ([Nathan Savant 2021, 12:18](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=738)).

### Pacing, momentum and skeletons

Generated plot also needs rhythm. Otto paces her output by walking the social graph edge by edge instead of picking edges at random: walking an edge brings both characters into the scene, the next edge may add a third or start a new scene, and those cuts make output read like chapters of prose rather than a raw event trace ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 12:11](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=731)). Ada Null keeps the deliberately bland generated text of Kiss Garden engaging with two event-level techniques, layering and rapid change: two narratives run at once and alternate every stanza, the dating narrator sees two or three people at a time, relationships last only a few dates, and the garden narrator shifts between wandering, pondering and obsessing over a plant ([Ada Null 2025, 7:26](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=446)).

McHorse and Foster's Hidden Door combines handwriting and generation differently: short, generic, handwritten trope structures form the skeleton, and LLMs give each a unique contextual expression. They chose tropes because meeting or subverting trope expectations satisfies players ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 21:45](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1305)).

Nat Alison names what generated content tends to lack. Alison, defending hand-made sudoku, says human-designed puzzles have a story: a core "break-in" deduction that flows through developing logic to a resolution, whereas computer-generated puzzles have no set path ([Nat Alison 2023, 10:47](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=647)). The same gap applies to plot: a generator can produce a valid sequence without a through-line. Setup and payoff are one way to supply it. In Dustin Freeman's live roguelike performance, a dragon rescued earlier becomes the escape route from a featureless final room, and a performer calls it out as Chekhov's gun ([Dustin Freeman 2023, 29:35](https://youtu.be/mXRKvbRi9qc?t=1775)); Capacle's surprise-with-coherence is the same effect produced by a system ([Cezar Capacle 2024, 10:09](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=609)).

### Choosing an approach

- **Simulation** gives surprise and player ownership, but beats are only hoped for ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 3:07](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=187)). Pair it with sifting (previous section) and with author-level goals if you need direction ([Max Kreminski 2019, 21:35](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1295)).
- **Planning** guarantees required beats and can explain and repair stories, at the cost of searching alternatives ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 20:11](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1211); [Stephen G. Ware 2025, 15:39](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=939)). It suits games with specific beats that must land.
- **Grammars and tropes** (quest parts, fail-forward complications, trope skeletons) are cheap to build and easy to author, but they repeat and need pacing rules ([Nathan Savant 2021, 1:44](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=104); [Cezar Capacle 2024, 18:13](https://youtu.be/NklQJfhZT3k?t=1093); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 21:45](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1305)).

## Borrowing responsibly: real symbols, cultures and the past

Roguelikes borrow freely: occult sigils for a spooky altar, a retro aesthetic, the conventions of old fantasy. Fiction built from real material carries real meaning, and the talks that address this ask you to know what you are borrowing.

### Real magic, real people

Stanley W. Baxton opens with a hypothetical: a horror developer researches "real magic", finds a scary-looking symbol, ships it, and has unknowingly shipped something antisemitic. Searching online mostly surfaces Western esoteric resources, which syncretise practices taken from specific cultures ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 2:19](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=139)). That tradition, the main source of "real" occult imagery in games, was built substantially through appropriation; Baxton names Aleister Crowley as continuing a habit of taking from many sources and Helena Blavatsky as inventing supposed Tibetan teachings, and people then put these symbols into games, comics and novels without knowing where they come from ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 3:22](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=202)).

He gives a set of tests while insisting there is no paint-by-numbers solution:

- **Ask why.** Does the symbol just look cool? Is what it represents in your game what it actually means, or what someone else decided it means? Talk to people from minority religions about how they want their practices depicted, if at all, and respect a refusal ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 10:22](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=622)).
- **Open or closed.** Find out whether a tradition is open (anyone may practise it) or closed (by invitation, often an ethno-religion). Closed traditions are often so tied to a culture that divorcing them strips their meaning; representing them almost always needs permission, which is often refused, frequently because of past disrespect from colonisers. Even open traditions need thought about context ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 7:43](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=463)).
- **Avoid symbols with Hebrew letters.** As a rule of thumb, Baxton says this sidesteps roughly 80% of appropriation. In his Baphomet example the central figure draws on an open Greco-Egyptian tradition, but the Hebrew letters come from Judaism's sacred language, and Jewish magic is not for outsiders ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 9:12](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=552)).

As a positive example he names Fallen London, which gets away with occult ideas partly by being set before Crowley's time and by using transformed or "if you know, you know" nods rather than full references. For diasporic practices such as Santería, the answer is to talk to living practitioners ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 15:29](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=929)).

### Owning your perspective

Xalavier Nelson Jr. widens the frame. Games have no special duty to be respectful, but they are not exempt from conveying a perspective, through how they are made and what they become. Decide what fun is, own the implications, and do not fixate to the point of paralysis. Asked about "realistic" sexism and racism in historical settings, he called it a decision like any other: if you want players to be uncomfortable, make sure you say it well ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 27:27](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1647)).

> They're not exempt from conveying a perspective through their creative process and through the final product. — [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 27:27](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1647)

### Nostalgia and dated sources

Retro aesthetics are a kind of borrowing too. Cara Esten Hurtle locates nostalgia's creative power in friction, the gap that opens when an aesthetic does not match the content people expect from it. Her HyperCard stack of nudes with text about her trans body, made in response to retrocomputing groups' no-NSFW rules, works that gap ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 7:26](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=446)). She also warns that reimagining the past through a retro aesthetic can wash over the real harms of the era; she cites critiques of Stranger Things making tolerance easy to imagine while the AIDS pandemic killed people in the background, and calls this reactionary even when it looks inclusive ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 6:22](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=382)).

Michael Brough takes a complementary line on old fantasy, the genre's source material. Engage with it despite its dated norms, because tracing how depictions changed gives a picture of progress and hope. He sets The Night Land, around 1912, with its completely helpless female character, against stories from the 1940s to 1960s where women throw daggers and hold their own ([Michael Brough 2025, 21:25](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1285)). Read together, Hurtle and Brough point in compatible directions: the past is useful material as long as you do not pretend its problems away.

### Resisting a single reading

Two talks address who gets to make meaning from generated work. Chelsea Thompto, a trans artist, builds systems populated with the texts, forms and feelings she wants viewers to confront, creating "spaces of contemplation" with legible themes that resist a single linear reading. That lets minoritised creators speak without their work being objectified or reduced to one message, and without producing "trauma porn" ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 1:21](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=81)). Alexandra Leonhart argues that a queer reading of games goes beyond representation, such as gay characters or pronoun options, to playing games queerly (speedrunning past designers' boundaries, friends inventing their own success metric in a racing game) and to queering the design process itself ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:06:19](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29179)). For a roguelike designer, both point to the generator as a place where a perspective lives, not only the characters on screen.

### A due-diligence routine

- For every real symbol, ritual or tradition you use, ask why, and whether your use matches what it means ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 10:22](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=622)).
- Find out whether the tradition is open or closed; for closed traditions, seek permission or leave it out ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 7:43](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=463)).
- Avoid occult symbols containing Hebrew letters ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 9:12](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=552)).
- Prefer transformed ideas and light nods over full references, and talk to living practitioners ([Stanley W. Baxton 2024, 15:29](https://youtu.be/HCbiYSzHtrI?t=929)).
- When you evoke a past era, decide what you are leaving out and whether that erases real harms ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 6:22](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=382)).
- Accept that the game conveys a perspective, and make it the one you intend ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 27:27](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1647)).

## Tensions and open questions

### Shaped arcs against open structure

Tarn Adams found Dwarf Fortress's adventure mode flat without an overarching structure and wants villains' schemes to supply plot ([Tarn Adams 2018, 1:25](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=85); [Tarn Adams 2018, 5:59](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=359)), and Matt Carney gives every run a spine in its pulse of descent ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1378)). Emilia Lazer-Walker abandoned culminating structures as more trouble than they were worth ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:19](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=979)), and Cole Wehrle's Oath has no beginning, middle or end by design ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 31:13](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1873)). Tim Keenan stands by leaving Duskers without a final resolution, but his players wanted one ([Tim Keenan 2017, 12:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=734)). The choice depends on whether the run already has a spine, on how predictable session length is, and on how much players have invested in the storylines you open.

### Emergence against required beats

The chapter's opening sections make the case for stories players assemble from what systems did ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 3:58](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=238); [Tarn Adams 2018, 7:18](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=438)). Stephen G. Ware's reply is that emergent agent stories can only hope to hit the beats a designer needs ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 3:07](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=187)), and Jasmine Otto found her tit-for-tat faction simulation interesting but impossible to steer ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 9:31](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=571)). Within the camp that does manage drama, three positions sit on one axis. Max Kreminski prefers to set state first and let events follow, calling a backfilled secret "cheating" for his own system ([Max Kreminski 2017, 20:46](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1246)); Ware's planners reason over possible futures and replan around the player ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 15:39](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=939)); Bad News has a human wizard who adds material whenever the simulation runs out ([Bad News team 2016, 39:55](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=2395)). The choice depends on whether your game has beats that must land, and on how much you are willing to intervene behind the player's back.

### The full record against the gap

Wehrle argues that a faulty, selective memory, together with regret, is the essence of good history-telling and that gaps make a record feel real ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 14:38](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=878); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 29:33](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1773)). Jonathan Lessard keeps every event and makes it browsable, and his leads come from what the full record reveals ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 5:22](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=322)). Caves of Qud and Dwarf Fortress keep a full record internally but show the player only fragments ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 49:44](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2984); [Isaac Karth 2019, 12:44](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=764)). The choice depends on whether investigating the past is the game, as it is for Lessard, or its backdrop.

### The power fantasy: keep it or take it away?

Jamie Brittain argues against prescriptive story structure and its bias toward happy endings, yet wants to keep the power fantasy that an overpowered run delivers ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 9:05](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=545); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 19:54](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1194); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 11:55](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=715)). Harry Solomons asks instead what is gained by withholding the time-loop's power fantasy, as Inscryption and Returnal do ([Harry Solomons 2024, 14:50](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=890); [Harry Solomons 2024, 18:10](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1090)). Andrew Cedotal adds that the anxiety a modern story should speak to is too many viable options, not resisting off-ramps on one path ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 25:13](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1513)). These positions follow from what the game is about: a power fantasy suits a game about getting stronger, and withholding it suits a game about loss.

### Justifying the restart

Marc Dolgin ties the need for an in-world reason to tone: comedy can skip it and serious games create the expectation ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 35:14](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2114)). Solomons treats leaving the restart unexplained as a legitimate choice that invites players' own conclusions ([Harry Solomons 2024, 24:30](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1470)), and Keenan's Duskers sidesteps the question by making the player at the keyboard the protagonist ([Tim Keenan 2017, 4:33](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=273)). No speaker says that one answer is always right.

### Attachment and permadeath

Lisa Brown grew so attached to her Road Not Taken character that her first permadeath ended her play ([Lisa Brown 2020, 22:14](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1334)), while Stella Vermilion's Nuzlocke runs build attachment through loss ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:56:18](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32178)). The difference seems to lie in whether loss is part of the expected shape of play. How much emotional investment a permadeath game can safely ask for is not settled.

### Fixed tone against grown tone

Jim Shepard sets tone up front and warns that abrupt shifts into dark drama backfire ([Jim Shepard 2016, 7:00](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=420); [Jim Shepard 2016, 25:26](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=1526)); Blaseball let its horror tone grow out of what the community responded to ([Joel Clark 2020, 25:24](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1524)). The choice depends on whether the game is a finished artefact or a live conversation with its players.

### Plain words against rich ones

Paul Dean, Francesco Cottone and Shepard argue for short, plain text and against walls of prose ([Paul Dean 2025, 4:53](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=293); [Francesco Cottone 2021, 7:08](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=428); [Jim Shepard 2018, 3:56](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=236)). Julian Day writes deliberate poetry, and Ivy Melinda credits Qud's purple prose with making its world feel alive ([Julian Day 2020, 10:15](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=615); [Ivy Melinda 2020, 4:34](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=274)). The practice the talks share is to keep text on the critical path brief and to put richness where curious players will find it, but how much richness a game can carry before it becomes a wall is a judgement each game makes.

### Optional story that still carries weight

Keenan wants curated story to supply goals and mystery yet stay optional ([Tim Keenan 2017, 1:48](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=108); [Tim Keenan 2017, 15:30](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=930)). Shepard warns that mandatory information placed in optional books may never be read ([Jim Shepard 2018, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=306)), and Jeff Lait believes no player found Vicious Orcs' hidden good ending on their own ([Jeff Lait 2025, 19:15](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1155)). Optional story is safe only when nothing the player needs depends on it.

### Unsolved problems

- **Drama against replay and agency.** Rich Wilson calls reconciling a replayable system with a dramatic story, and keeping a player from breaking planned drama, open problems that Prey: Mooncrash sidestepped rather than solved ([Rich Wilson 2021, 21:12](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1272); [Rich Wilson 2021, 22:06](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1326)).
- **Why would anyone care?** Lessard says accessible simulated history does not explain why players would care about thousands of fictional people, and does not claim to have solved it ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 7:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=429)).
- **Stories buried in the interface.** Kreminski notes that in dense simulations the compelling moments are buried and effectively closed to novices ([Max Kreminski 2020, 0:30](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=30)).
- **Unreliable narrators.** Sherveen Uduwana has found no roguelike that clearly uses repeated runs to give a Rashomon-like story whose objective truth players gradually work out ([Sherveen Uduwana 2022, 11:13](https://youtu.be/_w4yJsRzXBk?t=673)).
- **Centring emotion.** Dennis Greger says the conversation about building around genuine emotion is barely happening in games ([Dennis Greger 2025, 15:07](https://youtu.be/50u5_hXZkv4?t=907)), and Florence Smith Nicholls finds reality TV's confessional hard to translate into digital play ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 9:50](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=590)).
- **Persistent legends.** Thomas Biskup's idea of a killer resurfacing as a named nemesis in a later game was still on ADOM's to-do list ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 32:54](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1974)).
- **Rewriting what others say.** Courtney Liessen's rewritable NPC lines could be a game of their own and raise questions about rewriting someone's words for a better item ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 17:35](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=1055)).
- **How far worldbuilding goes.** Robin Mendoza agrees that asking why a dungeon has a shopkeeper unravels into worldbuilding with no obvious place to stop ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 13:46](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=826)).

## Checklist

1. What stories do players tell you about their runs, and which of your systems produced them?
2. Do your systems interlock, behave consistently and reward investigation, and is there room left for players to imagine?
3. What could you remove or leave unexplained so the player fills it in?
4. Does your game start players with a situation, keep disrupting it, and remember and call back what they chose?
5. Is there a place, such as a death screen, chronicle or journal, where a run becomes a story the player can keep or retell?
6. What story shape fits your run length, and does the run have a spine?
7. What does death mean in your fiction, does the restart need a reason, and what carries over between runs?
8. Does each mechanic make the player do what the story is about, and does its fiction match it?
9. What would a player conclude about your world from your numbers, categories and generators alone?
10. Can you state your tone in one line, and does every piece of text pass it?
11. Does your setting suggest mechanics and give generated content a shared key?
12. Is your text short where it must be read and rich only where curious players will find it?
13. Is authored story structured so it can be met across runs without branching beyond what you can write?
14. Does the game acknowledge what has happened to each character, including by chance?
15. Do you log, sift and surface the dramatic moments your simulation produces, and have you checked every real symbol, culture or era you borrow?
